title: Moonshot loop status
first_prompt: Inspect the state of the currently running moonshot loop -- share # of turns, tokens used so far, and summarize changes / issues

commits.summary: jvmcontract: a property check gives an interface parameter an implementation, reads accessors and Strings, and runs a HashMap model, for example 285 (verification pending)
commits.body:
Example 285 (CVE-2023-34055, Spring Boot's WebMvcTags.method(HttpServletRequest)) had every proof task refused before any proof (VF-027): a property check made no input of an interface type, its expressions had no String terms and read no interface, the fix resolves the method through a HashMap that HttpMethod's class initializer fills, and the gap scan of the fixed release ran into its two-minute limit. The verifier is extended so that the frozen claim is decided as stated, on the released JARs, with no wrapper and no narrower subject.

What changed in lib/:
- A parameter of an interface type is given an implementation (src/given.rs): a generated class that answers each accessor the target may call (an abstract method of no parameters returning an integer, a boolean or a String) with one value, the same on every call. It is an object made by its constructor, so the accessors' values are the harness's symbolic inputs; the domain line and the statement say what that covers, a witness reads `method(request=HttpServletRequest{getMethod()="TRACE"})`, and the interpreter and a JVM replay the same class file. A method it doesn't answer is a named gap, never passed over.
- A property's expressions read an interface's object through its accessors and a String by content: `result.getKey().equals("method")`, `request.getMethod() != null` (src/harness/expr.rs). A property check now takes a String inside any object it makes, as the regression check does.
- The own checker runs a model of java.util.HashMap (lib/models/java/util/HashMap.java: HashMap(), HashMap(int), put, get, containsKey, size, isEmpty), models String.hashCode, runs a modelled String method whatever class the call names (Object.equals, CharSequence.length), and reproduces Objects.requireNonNull and Pattern.compile of a constant regular expression of a plain form the JDK always compiles. Each has an evidence record in values::OPERATIONS, sampled by cases that must agree on a JVM, in the interpreter and in the checker; 28 operations outside the records are checked to stay named gaps.
- The gap scan follows a virtual or interface call into the classes of the objects it has seen made, not every class below the call's owner, classifies such a call once it has seen them all, and decides a class initializer in one memoized walk. The scan of example 285's fixed release went from over two minutes (its limit) to 0.04 s, and HttpMethod's initializer is no longer judged outside the fragment for what an unrelated Map of the class path does.
- The contract library's contract for HashMap.<init>(int) is taken out with its records: the call is the model's, no gap.

Verified inline: the default run, python3 lib/tools/test_costs.py run, 34 of 34 (cargo test and every Python suite), which includes the new lib/tests/interface_parameters.rs (a label bounded through an enum's map proved, the raw label and a claim that forgets a verb refuted on a JVM, what an implementation doesn't answer refused by name, the scan's dispatch), a unit test of the expression terms, and the values corpus, where every new case (String.hashCode, the map's seven calls over String and null keys and two keys of one hash, requireNonNull, Pattern.compile) gives the JVM's outcome in the interpreter and in the checker. On the cached JARs of example 285 and a debug build, the frozen assertion under --nullable request, --gaps strict and --max-array-length 8 was refuted on Spring Boot 2.7.17 (witness HttpServletRequest{getMethod()=""}, run on a JVM), established on 2.7.18 in 0.1 s, and refuted on the mutant; dropping a name from the assertion is refuted on 2.7.18, so the proof is not vacuous. Those inline runs are no receipts, and JBMC was not run.

Verification pending: jobs 20261115-173146-example-285-vulnerable-security-the-boun, 20261115-173146-example-285-fixed-security-the-bounded-m and 20261115-173146-example-285-mutant-security-the-bounded (the three tasks' ordinary attempts through build.py, the gap packets' closure test: the unchanged claim 196346d46d4d81fb on the same artifacts), 20261115-173209-conformance-corpus-under-jbmc-auto-and-a (the conformance corpus's proof tier, where JBMC runs the HashMap model) and 20261115-173209-object-comparisons-under-jbmc-and-auto-c (the object comparisons' proof tier, since the harness reads fields through a new emitter). Example 285's sidecar keeps its blockers until the receipts decide; its notes say what is queued. The preservation task is still blocked on the two dependency closures, which is next.

commits.summary: jvmcontract: a regression check runs each version on its own dependency closure and over an interface parameter, for example 285's preservation (verification pending)
commits.body:
Example 285's preservation task (Spring Boot 2.7.17 against 2.7.18, WebMvcTags.method(HttpServletRequest), the known-method-labels-preserved claim) was not executed: the two releases have dependency closures of other bytes, and jvmcontract's equivalence took one class path for both (VF-027's verifier-interface:two-dependency-closures). Behind that refusal a regression check also made no input of an interface type and compared two results of an interface type by Objects.equals, which says nothing about objects of two relocated classes. The regression check is extended so that the frozen claim is decided as stated, each release on its own pinned closure.

What changed in lib/:
- equivalence --before-classpath gives the previous version a dependency closure of its own (relocate::with_closure). Its build is relocated under before/ as always, and with it every class of its closure that the build names, directly or through the closure's classes in turn (a class entry, a descriptor or a generic signature of the constant pool), so both versions run in one program, each on its own libraries. A class only the new closure has is renamed in the previous version's references too, to a class that does not exist, so the previous version never runs on the new version's. Nothing is shared between two closures, JDK classes apart. Without the option both versions run on --classpath, as before.
- A parameter of an interface type is given an implementation in a regression check as in a property check (src/given.rs): one generated class per version, answering the accessors either version may call, the two objects made from the same values. A given implementation's fields are final, so nothing of it is compared after the calls.
- A result of an interface type that the previous version has its own copy of is compared through the interface's accessors, a String by content, two nulls agreeing; the statement says so. An interface with an abstract method that is no accessor, or with none, is refused by name (given::unread).
- --unchanged-unless reads a given object as Java does, on the new version's (request != null && !request.getMethod().equals("GET")). An input on which the expression throws is not among those the change is meant for, so the versions are compared on it. Such an expression beside an object made by its constructor is refused by name.
- JBMC is given neither a given implementation nor a closure of the previous version's own: --engine jbmc and --confirm are refused by name, as are --before-target, --before-arguments, --results-agree-when and a correspondence over an interface parameter.

examples/tools/targets/runtime.py passes the previous revision's dependencies as --before-classpath when the pair's closures differ, where it refused the pair before; a pair with one closure of the same bytes is run as before.

Verified by: lib/tests/interface_regression.rs (new, tool tier, a fixture of two library closures): a fix over an interface parameter proved preserved outside its declared change, refuted with no change declared, on a version that changes a known input and on one that reads a second accessor, each witness run on a JVM; a previous version that names a class only the new closure has is not verified; a declared change that throws on a null request compares that input; each refusal by name. Unit tests of the closure relocation, of the abstract methods accessors leave unread, and of the previous descriptor; the JBMC refusals in conformance.rs's pending test; a unit test of the route's command line for one closure, two and none. The default run passed, 34 of 34, before a last addition to the statement's words (the thrown declared change, only where a given implementation is among the inputs), after which the unit tests and the two interface test files were run again.

On the cached release JARs, inline, with the frozen allowed change, --nullable request, --gaps strict and --max-array-length 8: established in 0.1 s (0.8 s wall); refuted with no change declared (getMethod()="", run on a JVM).

Verification pending: job 20261115-181427-example-285-preservation-the-known-metho runs example 285's preservation task as stated (the gap packet's closure test, expected established), and job 20261115-181435-object-comparisons-under-jbmc-and-auto-c runs lib/tests/heap.rs's proof tier under JBMC at this commit, at low priority, since every regression check goes through the harness this changes. Example 285's three security jobs (20261115-173146-example-285-...) have passed, each as expected, and await collection; its sidecar keeps its blockers until the receipts are in the repository, and its notes say what is queued.

commits.summary: jvmcontract: under auto, JBMC is no fallback for a given implementation or a closure of the previous version's own
commits.body:
The regression check refused --engine jbmc and --confirm over a parameter given an implementation of its interface, and over a previous version on a dependency closure of its own (--before-classpath), but under --engine auto a run where the own checker had no verdict (out of time) would still have gone on to JBMC, which is given neither. It now stops there with a note, as it does for a String parameter: 'the tool's own checker gave no verdict, and JBMC is not asked: it takes an implementation of an interface the check gives, which only the own checker is given'. The assertions are in conformance.rs's test of the domains JBMC is not given (a looping method of the fixture, sourceTriangle, and a deadline of zero, for both cases); lib/tools' lint keeps a test that names JBMC out of the tool tier, which is why they are not in interface_regression.rs.

The second run of lib/tests/heap.rs's proof tier under JBMC, queued with the previous commit (20261115-181435-object-comparisons-under-jbmc-and-auto-c, about three hours), is withdrawn before it started: its job file is removed. It was to check that the regression harness is unchanged for inputs with no interface parameter and one class path. That is now shown directly: the 70 harness classes the heap tests' tool-tier proxies generate (57 regression, 13 property) are byte for byte the same at commit lvvpsuxl and at this one (a scratch build of that commit's lib/, sha256 of every harness class under target/tmp/heap*), and JBMC is running the proof tier on those bytes at lvvpsuxl (job 20261115-173209-object-comparisons-under-jbmc-and-auto-c). Withdrawing it also lets the pipeline collect example 285's preservation result (job 20261115-181427-example-285-preservation-the-known-metho, still pending) without waiting for three more hours of JBMC in the same run.

Verified by: the default run after the change passed 33 of 34, the one failure being the lint on where the new assertions first were (interface_regression.rs); after moving them, conformance.rs (10 passed, the changed test four times over), interface_regression.rs, interface_parameters.rs, values.rs, the unit tests and lib/tools' three lint suites were run again and pass.

commits.summary: Verification results for 6 jobs: example 285's four receipts pass, the conformance corpus passes, the object comparisons fail as in VF-018
commits.body: Ran 20261115-173146 (example 285 fixed, mutant, vulnerable: expected verdicts, outputs applied), 20261115-181427 (example 285 preservation, passed, outputs applied) and 20261115-173209-conformance (passed: JBMC and auto --confirm, 34m). 20261115-173209-object-comparisons (heap proof tier at 18cfa9e6) failed again on the same four tests as VF-018 (JBMC did not finish within 600 s), recorded there. 20261115-181435-object-comparisons was withdrawn by its submitter after it started and stopped; its leftover result was set aside, not collected (VF-029). Verified by pipeline.py status: nothing pending, running or uncollected.

commits.summary: Example 285 is decided: its four proof tasks have their receipts, each as expected, and its blockers are closed
commits.body:
Example 285 (CVE-2023-34055, Spring Boot's WebMvcTags.method(HttpServletRequest)) had every proof task refused before any proof (VF-027). With jvmcontract extended in the three commits before the pipeline's (lvvpsuxl, lustnxwm, oyvynrux), the unchanged claims were rerun on the released JARs by its own checker under strict gaps, and the pipeline collected the receipts in xkplwmyz: vulnerable-security refuted on 2.7.17 (witness request.getMethod() = "", the label ImmutableTag{key="method", value=""}, run on a JVM), fixed-security established on 2.7.18, mutant-security refuted on the mutant (the same witness), and preservation established between 2.7.17 and 2.7.18, each release on its own pinned closure. Each is as expected and not vacuous; the verifier's runs took 0.2 to 0.4 s.

This commit brings the example's records in line with the receipts. target.json lists no blocker (the four observed ones and the two predictions are removed) and its handoff says what is decided and what the claims leave open; each records/refusals/TASK.json keeps the refusal as it was observed and gains `closed`, naming the job and the receipt that decided the claim; example.json's summary, verdict label and notes say what was proved and about which domain (an implementation of HttpServletRequest that answers getMethod() with one non-null String of at most 8 code units, or a null request); the page's two blocker sections are replaced by 'The proofs' and 'Closed gaps'. The router and examples/gap-inventory.md are regenerated: 21 blocked obligations in five observed gaps, where there were 25; two-dependency-closures now blocks three tasks (286, 287 and 306's preservation, whose route no longer refuses them, so their rerun checks will fail as not predicted and their ordinary attempts will say what else each needs) and interface-parameter four (305's). VF-027 has a dated update saying so.

The tests that pinned the blocked state follow: test_gap_inventory.py's ranking, totals, dated predictions (285's two are gone) and closure tasks; test_workflow_refusal.py's table of blocked tasks (21), its rerun example (286's preservation, since 285's is decided), and a new test that a closed gap blocks nothing, predicts nothing, leaves the task executable and names a receipt that decided the unchanged claim as expected; test_acceptance.py accepts an earlier unresolved receipt of a task whose packet is closed. Verified by the Python half of the default run (32 of 33 suites, the one failure being the cost inventory's lint on the renamed tests, fixed with test_costs.py estimate and rerun with the three changed suites); nothing under lib/src or lib/tests changed since the last Rust run.

A correction to the previous commit's message (oyvynrux): it said the second heap proof-tier job, 20261115-181435-object-comparisons-under-jbmc-and-auto-c, was withdrawn before it started. The runner had started it at 18:25 UTC from the commit that queued it, before the commit that removed its job file landed; it was stopped, and its leftover result set aside (VF-029). The first one (20261115-173209-object-comparisons-under-jbmc-and-auto-c, at lvvpsuxl) failed on the four claims of VF-018, where JBMC does not finish in 600 s, as it did before these changes; its other five tests passed.

commits.summary: jvmcontract: claims javac compiles, String and String[] inputs, String, stream and regex models, induction and lemmas, for example 286's decision claim (verification pending)
commits.body:
Example 286 (CVE-2022-22968, Spring Framework 5.3.18 to 5.3.19) states its decision claim in Java over the adapter entry allowed(String[] allowedPatterns, String[] disallowedPatterns, String field): a field some disallowed pattern matches ignoring ASCII case is denied, the match written with streams, lambdas and java.util.regex. Until now jvmcontract refused it at the String[] parameters, at the expressions, and at every String, StringBuilder, stream and regex call on the way. With this change the unchanged claim is proved on 5.3.19 and refuted on 5.3.18 and on the constructed mutant at small bounds inline (3 code units and 3 elements: 8 s, 7 s and 6 s in an unoptimized build), each witness run in the harness on a JVM; the frozen bound of 8 is queued.

What a property check gained. A String parameter is a String of its own of at most --max-array-length code units, and a String[] an array of such Strings or nulls. An assumption or assertion the tool's own expression compiler does not take is compiled by javac into a class beside the harness and run as bytecode, as the target is; a witness of such a claim is run in the harness on a JVM, so a refutation rests on Java's own libraries and not on a model. prove --decreases EXPR proves a method that calls itself by induction on a measure: a recursive call on arguments within the assumption and the bound whose measure is smaller is taken to satisfy the property, and any other recursive call ends the check with no verdict. prove --lemmas FILE proves each lemma first and then lets its statement stand in for the calls of its method where the arguments are within the bound it was proved at, the method running as written elsewhere; a method that writes a field or compares its arguments by identity is refused as a lemma's subject.

What the own checker gained. String.substring, indexOf, endsWith, toLowerCase on ASCII (under the stated assumption that the default locale is not Turkish, Azeri or Lithuanian), split at one character and chars; StringBuilder's constructors, length, indexOf, substring, delete and toString; lambdas, method references and four stream model classes run as the loops they stand for; Pattern.quote, String.join, Pattern.compile, matcher and matches as far as a claim states a glob with them, a pattern held as its pieces so that a case-insensitive match and an exact match of lower-cased Strings are one formula; class literals, Class.forName and the class path's loader under a stated assumption, for spring-jcl's logging probes. Each new String method has an evidence record in values::OPERATIONS (String model 3) whose 85 boundary cases give one outcome on the JVM, in the interpreter and in the checker; the interpreter's substring and toLowerCase now return the JDK's objects (the String itself, the literal empty String). What a model takes for granted about the JVM is listed among a statement's assumptions.

Paths. Once more than 1024 paths have been explored (Options::merge_heaps_after), paths whose heaps are not of one shape are merged into the union of their heaps, each first rid of dead locals and unreachable objects; a loop's exit is then a join, and waiting paths are resumed in the order of the loops they are in. Below that count the engine merges as before. The count is a measured compromise: merging heaps from the first path took the values sweep's list totals from 0.07 s to over a minute at 6 lines, since the two sums are then no longer one formula by gate hashing, and waiting for 1024 paths costs example 286's decision 1.7 times its time at 5 code units against 512. An array of computed size is taken within one more than the bound (a table over a bounded String's positions).

Two leaks found by the default run and closed. The new StringBuilder, Class and ArrayList models had been added to gaps::exact_jdk_call, which JBMC's gap listing and the contract reader also ask: JBMC's stubs for those calls would have counted as exact, and a contract for StringBuilder.<init>() was refused. They are now gaps::modelled_jdk_call, the own checker's alone, and a contract given for a modelled call is applied in place of the model, so the three contract tests of lib/tests/integration.rs pass unchanged. And a call the checker has no model of on a builder it holds the content of (append, reverse) now drops that content: a later modelled call on the builder is refused by name instead of answering from stale content.

examples/286-.../proofs/prove.py TASK runs vulnerable-security, fixed-security or mutant-security from target.json and the frozen claim file, on the revision's pinned JARs (each checked against its SHA-256) with the adapter compiled against them, and builds the mutant as sources.lock.json says. proofs/simple-match.contract is the lemma: PatternMatchUtils.simpleMatch on ASCII Strings is the claim's own regular expression, by induction on the pattern's length. These are proofs beside the example route, which runs the verifier on the original artifact alone and still stops at DataBinder's receiver (VF-027); the example's records are not changed in this commit and follow with the results.

commits.summary: Example 286's decision claim is decided beside the route: established on 5.3.19, refuted on 5.3.18 and on the mutant, at the frozen bound
commits.body:
The three decision jobs queued with zrzuurtk have finished, each as expected, on the unchanged claim claims/disallowed-field-denied-ignoring-case.json through the adapter entry its first assumption names, with maxArrayLength 8, unwind 16, the own checker and strict gaps. fixed-security (job 20261115-234439-example-286-fixed-security-through-the-a): established on Spring Framework 5.3.19 in 920 s after the simpleMatch lemma's own proof in 92 s (4,889 paths, 2.6 million variables, 8.7 million clauses, 1.41 GiB), not vacuous; its trial at 6 took 189 s. vulnerable-security (20261115-234439-example-286-vulnerable-security-through): refuted on 5.3.18 in 409 s at allowed(allowedPatterns={"**", null, null, null, null, "", "", ""}, disallowedPatterns={"_Y[]*US"}, field="_Y[]  uS"), which returns true. mutant-security (20261115-234440-example-286-mutant-security-through-the): refuted on the constructed mutant in 398 s at allowed(allowedPatterns=null, disallowedPatterns={null, null, null, null, null, null, "*Y"}, field=" yzzy"). Both witnesses were run in the harness on a JVM (JDK 25.0.5), so the refutations rest on the releases' bytecode and Java's own java.util.regex, not on a model. The results themselves are collected by the verification loop; this commit cites them by job.

The example's records say what was decided and what was not. README.md has a section with the verdicts, the witnesses, how to rerun (python3 proofs/prove.py TASK), what the proof is (the lemma by induction, one meaning for a regular expression) and what the verdicts rest on (the lemma, the checker's models of the JDK calls on the way, and two stated assumptions about the locale and the class loader). example.json has four dated notes and a verdict label. In target.json the three predicted blockers the proofs reached each keep their text and gain a dated note saying they were reached and closed outside the route, the fourth (the bean wrapper's reflection) a note that it is still not reached, and handoff.next says what is next. VF-027 has an update line.

Not decided, and said so: these are proofs beside the route, not route receipts. The route runs the verifier on the original artifact alone, has no adapter entry and passes no lemma, so all six proof tasks stay blocked there, their packets and rerun checks unchanged. preservation, tried through the adapter entry, stops at the String[] parameter in the regression check; the protected-state tasks stop at java.util.ArrayList.<init>(int) in MutablePropertyValues.<init>, before the bean wrapper's reflection. The proof-tier job queued with zrzuurtk (20261115-234440-the-proof-tier-after-example-286-s-engin) is still running.

commits.summary: CLAUDE.md: a probe of a prover or model checker may run inline up to 5 minutes and 4 GB, under a cap
commits.body: At the user's request: the 1 GB line between inline runs and verification jobs had agents tuning a checker's memory to fit a quick probe before knowing whether the real proof works (prove-examples, example 287), and real-world claims often need more than 1 GB just to show where a checker stops. A single probe on one claim may now run inline, one at a time, for up to 5 minutes and 4 GB, inside systemd-run --scope with MemoryMax=4G and a timeout, so it cannot take more. A run that needs more is still a job, and the default test run and the tool tier keep their 1 GB. CLAUDE.md and verification/README.md say the same.

commits.summary: Verification results for 4 jobs: example 286's three claims pass as expected, the proof tier stops at heap.rs on VF-018's three timeouts
commits.body: Jobs 20261115-234439 (fixed-security: established; vulnerable-security and mutant-security: refuted, all as expected, applying their outputs) passed. The proof-tier job 20261115-234440 failed at lib/tests/heap.rs: three JBMC timeouts at 1800 s, the VF-018 tests, so the binaries after heap and the Python proof tests did not run (VF-030, VF-018 updated). Conformance passed.

commits.summary: jvmcontract: loops beyond the bound covered by invariants, constant regexes, text as bytes and digits, for example 287's bcrypt claims (verification pending)
commits.body:
Example 287 (CVE-2025-22228: BCrypt.hashpw ignores bytes past 72) asks whether checkpw rejects a password of more than 72 bytes for every valid stored hash. The tool's own checker stopped at the claim's regular expression, at the text-to-bytes calls and at bcrypt's loops, which go round 18, 512, 2^cost and 64 times against --unwind 16. It now runs the claims as they are written. A loop that goes round more often than the bound is covered by an invariant the checker finds and proves by induction (lib/src/bmc/loops.rs: what one iteration writes is set to any value, candidate facts about each written number are dropped until the rest is kept by an iteration, and the loop is shown to end by a counter or said not to be); a verdict names the loops so covered, a violation past one is believed only when its witness, the least violating input, reproduces on a JVM, and otherwise the answer is no verdict with the loop named. Also new: String.matches and Pattern.compile of a constant regular expression with classes, groups, alternatives and counts (lib/src/bmc/regex.rs); String.getBytes(UTF_8), MessageDigest.isEqual, Arrays.copyOf, Integer.parseInt and StringBuilder's charAt and appends (lib/src/bmc/bytes.rs, strings.rs); Object.getClass of an object the run made, String.toString, an initializer that keeps method references, and a throws clause whose condition javac compiles. The solver side defers clauses until a call depends on them, checks lazy divisions only in the cone a question reads, and shares a path's models by pages. The search for the least witness takes at most half the time the run has left, so a violation found late is not lost to it.

The String model is model 4, the reference calls model 2: getBytes, matches and toString have evidence records sampled on the JVM and in the checker (lib/tests/values.rs), the gap scan counts Pattern.compile of a constant in the checker's syntax as reproduced, and the interpreter's String.toString returns the String itself. Tests that relied on a class regex, toString or a builder append being a gap now use forms that still are (a reluctant or possessive quantifier, trim, append(CharSequence), append(long)); the calibration fixture's RegexGate uses a possessive quantifier and its records were remade. New tests: lib/tests/loops.rs (four, on a small fixture with the same loop shapes), three in lib/tests/claims.rs (each model against a definition written out in Java and sampled on a JVM), three unit tests in bits.rs. Verified inline by the default run (python3 lib/tools/test_costs.py run: 34 of 34 passed).

Example 287 has proofs/prove.py, which runs the three security tasks beside the route through the adapter entry the claim names, and a dated note. One capped probe (5 minutes, 4 GiB) proved the byte-array guard claim on 6.3.8 at the route's bound in 250 s with six loops covered; the probe on 6.3.7 found its violating path and ran out of time minimising the witness, and the probe of the security claim through the adapter did not finish. None of these is a receipt. Jobs: 20261116-053832-example-287-fixed-guard-the-byte-array-g and 20261116-053832-example-287-vulnerable-guard-the-byte-ar (through the route), 20261116-053832-example-287-fixed-security-through-the-a, 20261116-053832-example-287-vulnerable-security-through and 20261116-053832-example-287-mutant-security-through-the (prove.py), and 20261116-053833-the-proof-tier-after-example-287-s-engin (the proof tier with --no-fail-fast and VF-018's three heap tests skipped, as VF-030 asks). Not attempted: the preservation task.

commits.summary: Receipts keep the loops an invariant covers beside the checker's numbers; example 287's guard tasks are queued again (verification pending)
commits.body:
The first runs of example 287's two guard tasks through the route (jobs 20261116-053832-example-287-fixed-guard-the-byte-array-g and 20261116-053832-example-287-vulnerable-guard-the-byte-ar) ran the verifier to its verdict, in 4m42s and 6m00s at 2.2 GiB, and were refused when the receipt was checked: build.py copied everything in the checker's statistics into search.native, which the result schema keeps for numbers, and the statistics now carry the list of loops covered by invariants (and, since example 286, what the models assume). search_record keeps the numbers in native and the two lists in search.loopsCoveredByInvariants and search.modelsAssume, both added to result.schema.json, with a unit test in examples/tools/test_build.py.

test_packets.py read example 287's review note as the last of its notes, which the note added with the previous commit displaced: it now finds the note by the review item it names. That failure was in the previous commit, whose default run was made before the note was added. Verified inline by the Python half of the default run (33 of 33 after the fix; the Rust sources are unchanged since the full run before the previous commit).

The three security jobs of the previous commit passed and are not collected yet: fixed-security established on 6.3.8 in 641 s, vulnerable-security and mutant-security refuted on a candidate of 25 code units and 73 bytes with a hash of cost 04, run on a JVM. Jobs queued here: 20261116-06*-example-287-fixed-guard-again-for-its-receipt and 20261116-06*-example-287-vulnerable-guard-again-for-its-recei (the ids are in verification/jobs).

commits.summary: Example 287's public claim is decided beside the route: established on 6.3.8, refuted on 6.3.7 and on the mutant, at the frozen bound
commits.body:

commits.summary: Two modes of a checkout: development, and runtime on a user's machine
commits.body:
/prove-java-change will install a released copy of this repository on a user's machine. That copy must not trace, redact or publish anything, yet the agents working in it follow this repository's procedure, which says to commit with sync.py commit. So the procedure stays one and the checkout decides: llm-dlc/tools/mode.py tells a runtime checkout by a marker file at its root, .in-the-loop-runtime.json (written by the skill's bootstrap, gitignored, a fact about one copy), and anything else is a development checkout that behaves as it always has. IN_THE_LOOP_MODE overrides the marker for tests. A marker that can't be read is an error, never a development checkout, since tracing a user's sessions by mistake would publish them.

In a runtime checkout sync.py does this, decided before it takes its lock or writes anything under its state folder: commit writes the message with an In-The-Loop-Runtime: VERSION sha256:DIGEST trailer naming the release and starts a new change, reading no session; check passes with nothing to check; the hooks that run after every tool call and turn return at once; and every other command (push, upload, scan, sync, review, allow, stamp, langfuse, unpublish, regenerate) refuses and points at llm-dlc/runtime.md. In a development checkout one thing changes: link_commits never stamps a session's trace on a commit that carries the runtime trailer, so a contribution merged from a user's checkout is not credited to whichever session happened to be running when it was authored.

llm-dlc/runtime.md is the new page for the runtime side, starting with the two modes and the procedure for agents in a runtime checkout; CLAUDE.md and llm-dlc/README.md point at it. Examples added in a runtime checkout take numbers 900 to 999, which examples/README.md now reserves, so an update never brings an example with the same number.

Verified: test_mode.py (13 tests, in the cost inventory as unit tier) covers the marker, the override, each runtime command, main's dispatch without the lock, and the unstamped contributed commit. Run for real with IN_THE_LOOP_MODE=runtime: check exits 0, push exits 2 with the reason, hook exits 0 silently. Every Python suite passes (lib/tools/test_costs.py run --only python, 34 of 34 after test_performance.py's copied tool sources gained mode.py), and cargo test --test tiers, the Rust half of the tier lint. The rest of cargo test was not run again: no Rust file changed since the previous commit's full default run.

commits.summary: A release process with a hash, and the bootstrap that installs a release
commits.body:
/prove-java-change runs on a released copy of this repository, and the copy has to be the one the running skill was released with. A release is therefore one commit, the skill at a version and the repository beside it, pinned to each other by the sha256 digest of the commit's tree, which the skill carries in release.json beside its bootstrap. The pin can't name the commit's id, because it is in that commit, so it names the content: the digest is over one line per file (mode, sha256 of its bytes, path) and leaves out the pin itself and the files sync.py regenerates on every commit (llm-dlc/traces/, llm-dlc/index.json, llm-dlc/README.md), which the pin lists. It is of content only, so the trace lines sync.py adds to a commit's message later leave it as it was.

llm-dlc/tools/release.py cut [VERSION] is the one command a release takes, at any commit and as often as wanted: it writes the version into the plugin and the marketplace, the pin from @'s tree, commits with sync.py commit, and verifies the commit; it refuses while @ holds other uncommitted work. status and verify read the last release back. A release reaches users only when main is pushed with it.

plugins/in-the-loop/skills/prove-java-change/bootstrap.py is the user's side and the one implementation of the digest (release.py loads it). status says where things stand as JSON, install clones the repository with jj into IN_THE_LOOP_HOME (by default ~/.local/share/in-the-loop) and stands on the release, update fetches and rebases the user's commits onto the next release, listing conflicts. A release is found without a tag: through the history of the pin, for the commit that carries this version and digest, accepted only when its tree hashes to the digest again. A checkout is current only when that holds, the working copy descends from the release, and the skill's files in the release are the bytes of the skill that is running. Inside a development checkout the bootstrap answers development and installs nothing. The plugin's manifest and the marketplace entry come back with it, as plugin in-the-loop at 0.4.0; the skill's own page follows in a later commit, and no release is cut yet.

Verified: test_release.py, 11 tests (8 at the tool tier, with git and jj on a made-up repository in a temporary directory): the digest ignores messages and the files left out and sees a changed byte or mode; a commit changed after its digest was taken is no release; install stands on the release rather than the branch's tip, writes the marker and leaves git clean; a skill edited after it was installed blocks; a pin whose release is not in the repository installs nothing and leaves no directory; update moves a local commit onto the next release. On this repository the digest of 5,380 files takes 0.4 s. Every Python suite passes (35 of 35) and cargo test --test tiers; the rest of cargo test was not rerun, no Rust file having changed.

commits.summary: doctor.py: whether a machine can prove a change, and what blocks it
commits.body:
Step 1 of /prove-java-change has to say, in numbers, whether the user's machine is enough, and to tell what no setup can fix from what a setup fixes. llm-dlc/tools/doctor.py measures the machine and looks for the tools, installs and changes nothing, and gives each check one of three levels. Blocking: a proof can't run here; a hardware limit (under 8 GiB of memory, 2 CPUs or 10 GiB of free disk, a margin below the 8-core, 9 GB laptop that is the smallest machine this repository has run on) or an operating system other than Linux is blocking by itself, and so is a missing tool every proof needs (Python 3.11 with jsonschema, git, jj, a Java 25 JDK, cargo, and a Claude Code with the flags the loop uses). Limits: the machine works with less, and the check says what is lost (no JBMC, no systemd user scopes for memory caps, no JDK 21 and 25 under sdkman for replays, no Maven, gh or tmux). Ok otherwise. It exits 1 when something blocks, and --json gives the same as data.

It also proposes a budget, shared out as verification/README.md describes: a reserve for the person and the operating system, one loop's memory cap, and the rest to the verification runner, for whoever sets the machine up to adjust. For this VM (30 vCPUs, 105 GiB) the arithmetic gives the budget that was set here by hand on 2026-11-14: a 13G reserve, 12G for a loop, 80G and 26 CPUs for the runner.

Verified: test_doctor.py, 11 unit tests over made-up machines (which sizes block and which limit, that a limit says what is lost, that the three shares fit in machines from 8 to 512 GiB, the VM's budget, the exit status). Run on this machine: nothing blocking, nothing limiting. Every Python suite passes (36 of 36) and cargo test --test tiers; no Rust file changed, so the rest of cargo test was not rerun.

commits.summary: feature-loop.sh: a moonshot compacts at 600k tokens, and a compaction with no commit stops the loop
commits.body:
A moonshot has no acceptance criteria, so one context window is its measure. Each moonshot turn (named or templated, not a brief) now passes --autocompact 600k (FEATURE_LOOP_AUTOCOMPACT overrides it, 100k to 1M or auto). During the cycle's instruction, show_progress in loop-common.sh watches the stream for an automatic compact_boundary: if no commit has landed at @- since the cycle began, or since the previous such compaction, it ends the turn (SIGTERM to claude and its descendants), and the loop records 'Stopped ...: cycle N (item X) compacted with no commit at T tokens; session ... needs attention' and exits 1 for a person to look at. The session stays chained across cycles; manual /compact turns and the decide, status and summary turns are not watched. loop_stats.py counts the new ending as 'compacted, no commit'.

Verified with a stand-in claude on PATH that emits a compact_boundary event: an auto compaction with @- unchanged ends the turn at once, leaves no child behind and writes the reason; with a commit since, or a manual compaction, the turn runs to its end. claude accepts --autocompact 600k (checked against its argument validation). bash -n on both scripts; test_loop_stats passes. Written in workspace moonshot so the running prove-examples loop, whose bash has already parsed its loop body, is untouched; it takes effect from the next start of the loop.

commits.summary: prove-loop.sh: a proof loop forked from the session that prepared the example, with that session as its conductor
commits.body:
Step 3 of /prove-java-change. llm-dlc/tools/prove-loop.sh [--fork SESSION] [--memory SIZE] NNN... runs a new templated moonshot of feature-loop.sh, prove-change, over the examples it is given: the instruction of prove-examples, one example per cycle, on Fable 5.2 at high effort, every example given whether an earlier run committed for it or not. With --fork the loop's session starts as a fork of the session that prepared the example: the parent's transcript is found wherever that session ran, copied beside this checkout's sessions for one turn that runs without tools or the repository's hooks, and removed; the fork is then compacted and the cycles follow in it, so the loop needs no brief. The script starts the verification loop for the jobs the proof queues unless one already runs for the same jj repository, gives the queue an hour to clear after the loop ends, and keeps the run's state in llm-dlc/loop-summaries/prove-change/. It works the same in a development and a runtime checkout.

The conductor. The commit below this one (brought into this line from the moonshot workspace, where it was waiting) makes a moonshot's session compact itself at 600k tokens and stops the loop at a compaction with no commit. That rule can't tell hard work going well from a stuck session, and the conductor loop planned for it is superseded: the session that starts a proof loop conducts it. With LOOP_CONDUCTOR set, which prove-loop.sh does, the loop's reader appends the compaction to events.jsonl, lets the turn go on, and waits FEATURE_LOOP_CONDUCTOR_WAIT seconds (900) for a verdict. llm-dlc/tools/conductor.py wait blocks until there is such an event or the loop has ended, and decide N continue|stop --reason answers it. continue lets the turn run to its next compaction and is noted under the cycle's line in the run's record; stop, or silence, ends the turn and the loop as the rule alone does. A turn that ends by itself first takes its question back. Every other loop is unchanged: without LOOP_CONDUCTOR the rule stands as it was.

feature-loop.sh also gains FEATURE_LOOP_UNCAPPED=1, to run with no memory cap on a machine without systemd user scopes, where it otherwise refuses to start; it says so loudly. llm-dlc/runtime.md describes the loop and the conductor, and llm-dlc/README.md lists the loop with the others.

Verified with a stand-in claude, no model called: test_prove_loop.py (8 tool-tier tests, about 6 s) runs prove-loop.sh, feature-loop.sh and the reader for real in a made-up jj repository under a temporary CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR, and checks the fork's arguments and that the parent's copy is removed, the compact, the one-line instruction on claude-fable-5-2 at high effort with --autocompact 600k, a fresh session without --fork, a compaction that goes on at the conductor's word with its note in the record, one that stops at its word, one that stops for want of a verdict, a question taken back, a cycle with no commit, and an example that isn't there. test_conductor.py (10 unit tests) covers the event file and the verdicts. Forking a session that is mid-turn was tried by hand earlier with a real claude on a scratch folder; no real proof loop has been run through this yet. Every Python suite passes (38 of 38) and cargo test --test tiers; no Rust file changed.

commits.summary: contribute.py: what of a runtime checkout's work can go upstream, and a check of a prepared pull request
commits.body:
Step 4 of /prove-java-change ends by offering to send upstream what a proof added to the tool. A runtime checkout's commits have no traces, so they can't follow this repository's own commit procedure; llm-dlc/runtime.md now has the process that is theirs, and llm-dlc/tools/contribute.py is the part of it that can be checked by a program. It only reads: preparing the branch and opening the pull request stay with the agent, and only after the user agrees.

contribute.py status lists the commits made since the installed release and says of each changed path whether it travels (the library, the tools, the schemas, their tests and documentation), stays (verification/jobs, verification/results, the findings register and the priorities, traces, loop records and session notes: the machine's own record, which upstream runs again), or is an example, with its number. contribute.py check REV takes a prepared contribution, the commits from the upstream main to REV, and names each thing that stops it: a conflict, a commit without the In-The-Loop-Runtime trailer or with a session's trace trailer, a path that stays, an example still numbered 900 to 999, an example that names a file:// URL or an absolute local path as a source, and any added line that names the user's home directory, user name or host name. It says where such a line is and never prints it. With no problem it prints a pull request body: the release the work was built on, the commits, and what was not run.

Verified: test_contribute.py, 10 unit tests over made-up commits and diffs (the classification, added lines and their place, a naming line found and not quoted, a short or generic user name not searched for, a local source, a clean contribution, each stopping problem named). status run here answers that this is a development checkout. No pull request has been prepared with it yet. Every Python suite passes (39 of 39) and cargo test --test tiers; no Rust file changed.

commits.summary: /prove-java-change: the skill
commits.body:
The skill that replaces /verify-bytecode and /add-tla-model, and supersedes the planned conductor loop: plugins/in-the-loop/skills/prove-java-change/SKILL.md, in the plugin in-the-loop beside its bootstrap. It proves a change to Java code on a user's machine in four steps and is kept short on purpose, since it is locked to Fable 5.2 at high effort and runs inside this repository: it says what each step is for and when to stop, and the repository holds the rest. Step 0 asks the bootstrap where it is. Step 1 (set up, verify and measure the machine) is skipped when the checkout is current and doctor.py finds nothing blocking, and otherwise goes to one subagent on Opus; a hardware limit ends the run; the user confirms. Step 2 (assess the change, add the example with its claims, run it once on a JVM) stays in the orchestrating session, because the proof loop is forked from it; the user confirms. Step 3 starts prove-loop.sh --fork with the session's own id and conducts the loop from outside. Step 4 reports each claim as established, refuted or left open and offers to send what the proof added to the tool upstream. The orchestrator decides what it can and asks only for what is the user's.

In this repository the skill is also a project skill: .claude/skills/prove-java-change is a link to its folder in the plugin, so /prove-java-change NNN runs the copy being worked on, the bootstrap answers development, steps 1 and 2 are skipped and the skill goes straight to the loop on an existing example. Installed as a plugin it is /in-the-loop:prove-java-change. llm-dlc/runtime.md opens with a table of the four steps and what each stands on, and the top README has a section for the skill with how to install it.

Two things the page is honest about. release.py status now exits 1 while the skill's folder differs from the last release, because the plugin is installed from the tip of main and a copy of the skill that is not its release's bytes refuses to run: a change to the skill is followed by a cut before main is pushed. And a change that is not public has no route yet: a revision is prepared from a commit on github.com or a published JAR, so a private or uncommitted change is a blocker at step 2, or a fixture when it is small enough to copy; a local repository as a revision's source is the next piece of work, left out here because it changes the downloads policy and the files the running prove-examples loop works in.

Verified: claude plugin validate passes for the marketplace and the plugin; the bootstrap run through the project skill's link answers development with this checkout as home; every Python suite passes (39 of 39) and cargo test --test tiers. Not verified: the skill has not been run, in development mode or installed. That waits for the prove-examples loop to finish, as agreed, since a run starts a second proof loop on this machine.

commits.summary: feature-loop.sh: a compaction with no commit stops a moonshot only on a conductor's word, or with FEATURE_LOOP_STOP_ON_COMPACT=1
commits.body:
This line carries a copy (srxmyvov) of the change that made a moonshot compact at 600k tokens and stop at a compaction with no commit. The original, uzporttn in the moonshot workspace, was amended on 2026-11-15 at the user's request: the stop became opt-in, because cycle 2 of the prove-examples run compacted with no commit while making good progress, so the rule would have stopped good work. This commit brings this line to the same behaviour and fits the conductor to it, so that uzporttn can be abandoned at the merge instead of merged.

A moonshot's compaction with no commit since the cycle began, or since the last one, now has three outcomes. With neither setting, it is logged and nothing else happens, as in the amended uzporttn. With FEATURE_LOOP_STOP_ON_COMPACT=1 and no conductor, the turn ends and the loop stops, the old rule. With LOOP_CONDUCTOR, which prove-loop.sh sets, the conductor is asked: its stop ends the turn and the loop, and its continue lets the turn run to the next compaction. What changes for the conductor is its silence: no verdict by the deadline used to stop the loop and now leaves the turn running, with a line in the run's record, unless FEATURE_LOOP_STOP_ON_COMPACT=1 is also set. A conductor that has gone away, such as an orchestrating session the user closed, is then no worse than no conductor, and can't cause the false stop the amendment removed. The question is asked again at the next compaction with no commit. The header of feature-loop.sh, conductor.py's description, llm-dlc/runtime.md and llm-dlc/README.md say the same.

Verified with the stand-in claude: test_prove_loop.py has 11 tool-tier tests (8.5 s), four of them new or changed: silence from the conductor lets the turn go on and is noted under the cycle's line; silence with the rule on stops the loop; feature-loop.sh run by itself, with no conductor, only logs the compaction and the turn runs to its own end; and with the rule on it stops at the compaction. The conductor's continue and stop are tested as before. Every Python suite passes (39 of 39) and cargo test --test tiers. The skill's folder is unchanged, so release 0.4.1 stands; this commit is in no release yet.

commits.summary: README: the repository's page is about /prove-java-change, and each part's page carries its own layout
commits.body:
The repository's primary purpose is now the plugin, and the top README still introduced a set of demos with the skill as its last section. It is rewritten around the skill, at the user's request and with the work-in-progress landing page for the skill in the website's repository as a model for the order (that page was only read): what the skill does in three sentences and the command; how to install it and the four steps, with the two confirmations; what it needs (Linux, 8 GB, 2 CPUs, 10 GB of disk, Claude Code with Fable 5.2) and that it takes changes on GitHub only; the three answers a claim can get and that a model checker gives them, not the model; example 285 as the proof loop's first real target, with its three verdicts and its witness as the example's page records them; then a short table of what is in the repository, a few lines for agents (CLAUDE.md, the two modes, find.py, the job queue, the skill in this repository), the background and the licence.

The README no longer lists paths inside the folders: the four tables of files it had are gone, and each row of its one table links the part's page and that page's own layout. commits.summary: /prove-java-change takes a list of changes, orders them by how accessible they are, and prepares without proving with --scaffold-only
commits.body:

Step 2 understands and sizes every change, orders them with the most accessible first (a proof that lands early can extend the verifier under the later ones), and adds the examples in that order on the next free numbers from 900, so the numbers carry the order and no separate record of it exists. Each example's provenance is the request it came from and its notes hold what the preparation learned, because its proof may start in a session that never saw the preparation. A change that can't be prepared is set aside with its reason and the others go on.

--scaffold-only ends the skill after step 2, with every example a committed, reproducible scaffold (the readiness the examples' index already calls scaffolded) and no proof started. The same request without the flag proves what was prepared: nothing remembers a request, step 2 finds each change's example by its source and revisions and prepares only what has none. Step 3 then gives prove-loop.sh the examples still to prove, in order, in one run (one per cycle, in one session, as before) or, if the user prefers, one example per run with a report between. In a development checkout the examples named are taken in the order given.

New tool llm-dlc/tools/changes.py, read-only: it derives each example's state from its folder alone through examples/tools/targets/workflow.py (unprepared with the reason, prepared, decided, or unknown for an example with no target sidecar), lists a runtime checkout's examples 900 to 999 by number or the named ones in the order given, and with --pending prints the numbers still to prove as prove-loop.sh's arguments. commits.summary: /prove-java-change checks what else Claude Code has loaded, and the sessions it starts load only the checkout
commits.body:
Step 1 of the skill now checks the user's Claude Code setup on every run. It asks Claude Code itself: two one-word sessions on the smallest model, without tools or a transcript, one started as the user's session was (its directory and launch flags, read from the process CLAUDE_PID names) and one clean in the checkout, compared by what each reports at start-up; memory files, hooks and the plugins Claude Code's own listing calls enabled are added from disk. It prints names and paths only, never a setting's value.

Disabling is done by launch flags, not by editing the user's configuration, so nothing has to be put back: --setting-sources project,local, --strict-mcp-config, ENABLE_CLAUDEAI_MCP_SERVERS=false, and claudeMdExcludes for the memory files of the user and of the directories above the checkout. In a runtime checkout every session the skill starts now uses them (loop-common.sh's isolation: the proof loop's fork, compactions and cycles, and the verification loop's runs), and check proves on the machine that such a launch answers. The session the user is already in can't unload what it holds, so when anything is listed the skill offers the one command check prints (claude_setup.py launch: a clean session in the checkout, on Fable 5.2 at high effort, where the skill runs as the checkout's project skill) or, not recommended, to continue as it is. prove-loop.sh --no-isolation starts the loop's sessions as a plain claude for a machine where a clean launch does not work. Verified: test_claude_setup.py (21 tests, the check itself against a stand-in claude and made-up directories) and two new tests in test_prove_loop.py (in a runtime checkout all five sessions of a run carry the clean flags; with --no-isolation or in a development checkout none does). With the real Claude Code 2.1.325, from scratch directories: the flags leave no MCP server, connector, user skill or plugin in the start-up report, a memory file excluded by path is not read while the checkout's own is, the checkout's project skills still load, the login still works, and launch started from another project answers with the checkout's memory and not that project's. commits.summary: feature-loop.sh: a templated moonshot keeps an item for as many cycles as it takes, until a judge outside the session finds it finished, and "item" stops the loop once the item under way is
commits.body:
At the user's request: complex examples can take more than one cycle, but a templated moonshot gave each item exactly one, moving on as soon as a cycle committed (prove-examples left 286 with tasks open), and "stop" could only end the loop after a cycle, not after an example.

Now, after each commit of a templated moonshot, a judge outside the session decides whether the item is finished: a separate claude -p call (FEATURE_LOOP_JUDGE_MODEL, claude-sonnet-5-5 by default) with no tools, only the user's settings and no transcript reads the cycle's final report and commit messages and answers ITEM: finished (the goal is met, or what is left needs a person or only waits on jobs) or ITEM: continue (the session itself can still make real progress). Nothing is added to the moonshot's own session, so its instruction stays the only thing it is given. An unfinished item gets the next cycle with the same instruction; an unclear answer moves on, as before. The record keeps the verdict and its reason under each commit line, and a later run resumes at the first item that has no commit or whose last verdict was continues. FEATURE_LOOP_ITEM_CYCLES caps an item's cycles in a run (no cap by default, the user's choice), and FEATURE_LOOP_ITEM_JUDGE=0 restores one cycle per item. Typing "item" in the loop's terminal ends the run once the item under way is finished, however many cycles that takes; a count typed after it replaces it. loop_stats.py reads the new record header and verdicts, so an item the judge left open counts as attempted, not done, and the verdict is not published as a column.

Verified: test_loop_stats (22, two new) and test_runs pass, and the cost lint agrees. End to end, in a scratch jj repo with a stand-in claude that commits and answers as the judge from a script, the patched script (its own three-item list, no systemd scope): the judge kept item 1 for two cycles and the run went on to 2 and 3 and ended with no items left; a record whose last verdict was continues resumed at that item; an unclear answer moved on; a cap of 2 moved on after two continues; FEATURE_LOOP_ITEM_JUDGE=0 kept the old header and one cycle per item; a bad cap exits 2; and "item" typed during cycle 1, on a private tmux server, ended the run after cycle 2, once the judge found item 1 finished. Three real judge calls on made-up reports answered finished for a decided example, continue for one with work the session could do, and finished for one blocked on a person's decision.

commits.summary: feature-loop.sh: a conductor judges each cycle, an item that waits on its proof lets the next one start, and the loop asks before it changes items
commits.body:
This folds the moonshot branch into the /prove-java-change line. The commit below this one is a duplicate of tlzowkqv (workspace moonshot: an item keeps a templated moonshot until a judge outside the session finds it finished), with its six conflicts against this line resolved; this commit reconciles and extends it. The user asked on 2026-11-16 for everything about moonshot loops from the moonshot and conductor branches to be folded in here, for the loop to be run by a watcher session, and for a loop that goes on while an example waits on its final proof.

With a conductor directory (LOOP_CONDUCTOR, which prove-loop.sh sets) the conductor is the judge: after each commit the loop asks it whether the item is finished, takes another cycle, or only waits on the verification jobs it queued, and falls back on tlzowkqv's own judge (Sonnet, now with the third answer) when no verdict comes in FEATURE_LOOP_JUDGE_WAIT seconds. An item that waits is left: the loop takes the next one meanwhile, and whenever it leaves an item it first returns to the earliest waiting one whose jobs are in (conductor.py unfinished reads the queue and matches jobs to examples by their outputs or title). When only waiting items are left it waits for the first to come in. FEATURE_LOOP_CONTINUE_WHILE_PROVING=0, or prove-loop.sh --wait-for-proofs, keeps the loop on the item instead; the default is on. Between two items the loop asks the conductor whether to stop there, and waits longer while the run's merge-queue names a workspace the conductor is to merge first. The conductor can leave command lines (stop, item, counts) that the loop applies as if typed in its terminal, and the loop notes where it is as events (cycle-start, item, proofs).

So that a merge between two examples can't rewrite the script under the loop, feature-loop.sh and prove-loop.sh now run from a private copy of themselves. prove-loop.sh gains --session SESSION, which continues an existing session instead of forking one, and records its pid in run.json. In a runtime checkout the judge takes the clean launch flags instead of --setting-sources user. loop_stats.py reads the waiting verdict as an item left open, and knows the new endings.

Verified: test_prove_loop.py runs the loop against a stand-in claude, now also a stand-in judge and a made-up job queue (26 tests): the watcher's verdict keeps or ends an example, silence falls back on the judge, an example that waits lets the next start and is taken up again when its jobs are in (order 901, 902, 901, 903), the loop waits when only waiting examples are left, waiting with nothing outstanding is another cycle, --wait-for-proofs removes the third answer, a stop between examples and a queued merge's longer wait, a command line, --session, and a script rewritten mid-run that does not affect the loop. test_conductor.py has five new tests (15). The Python half of the default run passes, 41 of 41 suites. Not verified: any of this with a real model in the loop; the Rust tests were not run (nothing in lib/ changed). The pages (runtime.md, the skill) still describe the previous design and are rewritten with the watcher in the next commit, which also cuts the release.

commits.summary: /prove-java-change is started by a watcher on Opus 5.5, which starts each stage in a session of its own and watches the proof loop
commits.body:
The skill's session no longer does the work. It is the run's watcher (Opus 5.5, high effort; the user set the models on 2026-11-16) and starts, in order: the setup of the machine (a new session, Opus 5.5 high), the evaluation and ordering of the changes (the fixed session, Fable 5.2 medium), the setup of the examples from the evaluation's plan (a new session, Opus 5.5 high), and the moonshot loop over them, which continues the fixed session at high effort. llm-dlc/tools/watch.py is the watcher's tool: stage evaluate|setup (a headless session on its model and effort, clean in a runtime checkout), verification start|stop|status, loop (prove-loop.sh detached, with --session), wait (blocks until a question of the loop's, a proof that came in, the loop's end, or a summary when the interval has passed: 600 s by default, set with interval), summary and status (from llm-dlc/watch-summary-template.md, with what changed since the last summary first: examples that changed state, claims answered, commits, jobs queued or in; then the loop, the example under way, the verification jobs and what needs attention, such as a session silent for 20 minutes), merge add|done|list (workspaces the user asked to have merged between two examples), stop-after example|cycle|never, and proof NNN (the shell that waits on one example's proof while the loop works on the next). llm-dlc/prove-plan-template.md is the plan the evaluation fills in and the setup turns into examples.

SKILL.md is rewritten for the watcher, and llm-dlc/runtime.md has its section (the stages' briefs, watching the loop, the three questions and their defaults, merging between examples, what the watcher may fix); README.md and llm-dlc/README.md follow. claude_setup.py's clean launch now defaults to Opus 5.5, the watcher's model.

commits.summary: feature-loop.sh: a moonshot compacts at 600k tokens, and every compaction is logged
commits.body:
Each moonshot turn (named or templated, not a brief) now passes --autocompact 600k, so a long item has more room before compacting than Claude Code's default (about 470k for these sessions); FEATURE_LOOP_AUTOCOMPACT overrides it (100k to 1M, or auto). show_progress in loop-common.sh prints each compaction with its trigger and size, so whoever watches the loop sees it.

Opt-in, off by default: with FEATURE_LOOP_STOP_ON_COMPACT=1, an automatic compaction during the cycle's instruction with no commit since the cycle began, or since the previous such compaction, ends the turn (SIGTERM to claude and its descendants), and the loop records 'Stopped ...: cycle N (item X) compacted with no commit at T tokens; session ... needs attention' and exits 1. It is off because a compaction alone doesn't say whether the work is stuck: the prove-examples run's cycle 2 compacted with no commit while making good progress. Until a conductor judges this from outside the loop, a person watching does. loop_stats.py counts that ending as 'compacted, no commit'.

Verified with a stand-in claude on PATH emitting a compact_boundary event: without the opt-in the compaction is only logged and the turn runs on; with it, the turn ends at once with no child left behind and the reason written; with a commit since, or a manual compaction, it runs to its end. claude accepts --autocompact 600k. bash -n on both scripts; test_loop_stats passes. Written in workspace moonshot, beside the running prove-examples loop, whose bash has already parsed its loop body.

commits.summary: /prove-java-change takes examples that are already prepared, checks them before it starts, and the proof loop's text may be the user's
commits.body:
A request may now name examples by number in place of changes: ones an earlier --scaffold-only run, another agent or a person prepared. Stages 2 and 3 don't run for them. The watcher checks them all first with the new watch.py preflight NNN ..., which reads only the files and says for each example what it lacks, of two kinds: artifacts a proof needs (a revision that does not materialize from its lock, no validated replay) and faults in its form (example.json against its schema, a sidecar that does not load, a claim not frozen, no proof task). Exit 0 means nothing is lacking and the loop takes the examples in the order given, leaving out any already decided; exit 1 means something is, and the watcher makes one attempt to put it right with a setup session (Opus 5.5, high effort) under 'The repair's brief' in llm-dlc/runtime.md, checks again, and aborts with nothing started if anything is still lacking; exit 2 means an example is not there at all, and it aborts at once. A repair may write a missing claim only where the example's own pages state it in words, and the watcher shows such claims to the user before the loop starts. changes.py now reports what an unprepared example lacks by kind (gaps), which the check reads.

--instruction "TEXT" in the request gives the proof loop the user's own text in place of 'Formally prove example {} as elegantly and efficiently as possible': prove-loop.sh --instruction, FEATURE_LOOP_INSTRUCTION for feature-loop.sh's prove-change. It is one line with {} where the example's number goes, refused otherwise before anything starts, still the only thing the session is given, and kept in run.json and the run's record. In development the skill takes this path for the examples it is given, where it went straight to the loop before.

Verified with stand-ins and fixtures only: test_watch.py (27 tests: prepared, decided, a missing artifact, a broken sidecar, a schema fault, an absent example, one without a sidecar), test_changes.py (17), test_prove_loop.py (28: the user's text reaches every cycle and the record; a text without {} starts nothing), the Python default run (45 of 45 suites) and the Rust tier test. commits.summary: JBMC runs get a second attempt on Z3 with multiplication congruence lemmas, for VF-018 (verification pending)
commits.body:
Three regression proofs over objects (objects.Kernel#price, lines.Lines#reprice, orders.Orders#reprice) never finished under JBMC within 1800 s: finding VF-018, open since 2026-11-07. Each relates products whose operands are equal only under the correspondence or a branch, such as cents * quantity against quantity * cents. JBMC's SAT backend builds every multiplication as a circuit of its own, so its solver has to find each equality through two 64-bit multipliers. The diagnosis came from another agent's analysis the user passed on; it was reproduced here before anything was built on it: Z3 gives no answer in 60 s on JBMC's formula for the lines case and answers unsat at once with the lemmas, and with JBMC driving Z3 the three proofs take 0.11 to 0.14 s.

The change is in the tool, not in the tests or the harness. lib/src/congruence.rs reads a formula JBMC wrote as SMT-LIB and adds, for every two products of one width, the lemma that equal operands in either order give equal products, which holds of any fixed-width multiplication; nothing else in the formula changes. jbmc::run uses it as a second attempt: a run still without a verdict after a twentieth of its limit (5 s at least, 30 s at most) is held still with SIGSTOP (tla::run_with_interlude), JBMC writes its formula, and JBMC runs again with a solver script that answers that one formula, byte for byte, by giving Z3 the formula with the lemmas. Only a proof with every property holding is taken. Then the result names what decided it (its checker reads 'JBMC 6.11.0, its formula decided by Z3 5.3.3 with 6 multiplication congruence lemma(s)', its evidence names Z3, and it carries the counts). Anything else leaves the held run to go on with the time it had: JBMC can't write a trace as JSON from an SMT model, so a counterexample always comes from its own solver. Without a Z3, or with JVMCONTRACT_Z3=off, a run is as it was. doctor.py lists z3 as a tool whose absence limits what JBMC can prove.

Verified by the default test run (Rust and Python; the first run showed the attempt firing 50 ms into the short staged runs of two conformance tests, which is why it now waits 5 s at least), with unit tests of the reader and the lemmas and stand-in tests of a proof taken, a counterexample not taken with the run resumed where it was, and runs that never meet the attempt. One probe through jbmc::run with the real JBMC and Z3: lines.Lines#reprice ended Verified in 30.2 s (6 lemmas over 4 products, the attempt itself 0.2 s), and its defect twin was refuted by JBMC's own solver in 0.1 s as before. Not yet shown: the nine proof-tier tests of lib/tests/heap.rs, unchanged. Job 20261116-144006-vf-018-the-heap-proof-tier-under-jbmc-an runs them at the 600 s limit and is the finding's closing condition; VF-018 stays open until it is in. The prices test has proofs that are hard for Z3 too and may still need the longer limit.

Before the first real run of the skill (examples 288 onwards, in this development checkout), the user asked for four things. The watcher's summaries come every 30 minutes by default instead of 10, since nobody reads them as they come and each adds to the watcher's context; --summary-interval SECONDS in the request, or watch.py interval, sets another. The skill no longer forbids the model to start it, so the user can ask an open session for a run in their own words; its description says to start it only when the user asks. The run is to be as autonomous as it can: --unattended has the watcher read the claims of the catalog entries it had set up in the user's place, and accept them with watch.py claims NNN --accept REASON, which writes a decision for each example into the run's decision record, flagged as costly so the user reviews it afterwards; an example whose claims the watcher is not sure of is left out and reported. That flag is my reading of 'autonomous as possible': without it the run still waits for the user's one confirmation of the claims. And --record-as NAME (prove-loop.sh, FEATURE_LOOP_RECORD_AS) files a run under another loop's name, so 288 onwards are counted with 285 to 287 as prove-examples.

Found on the way: watch.py loop handed its arguments to argparse, which took the options out from between their values, so --memory 12G --wait-for-proofs 288 reached prove-loop.sh as --memory --wait-for-proofs 12G 288. One option worked, which is all the tests had; two or more would have failed the first real run. The arguments now go through in the order given. prove-loop.sh also took the window an ended loop was started in for a running verification loop, as watch.py did before its fix. In a development checkout the skill now runs the doctor for the loop's memory cap, and the catalog entry's brief says that a preparation over the inline limits is queued and waited for.

The user also asked that a clean launch never drop the memory of the project's own folder. It does not: probed on Claude Code 2.1.325 in a scratch folder with made-up markers, a session started with the clean flags held the folder's CLAUDE.md and its auto memory and not the CLAUDE.md of the directory above. runtime.md and claude_setup.py now say that the checkout's own memory always stays, and a test holds the flags to it. The user's own memory file was not in the probe, as this machine has none.

commits.summary: A queued verification job starts at once: the commit announces it, a runner at work takes it into its run, and results are collected as they come (verification pending)
commits.body:
Until now the verification loop looked at the queue every 60 seconds while it waited, and not at all while a run was under way: pipeline.py run read the queue once, at its start, so a job committed during a long proof waited for that proof to end, and every result of a run was collected only after its longest job. The user asked that the prover, the watcher and the verifier work the queue together, with the intervals kept as the backup. The parts: (1) pipeline.py run reads the queue again at once after a nudge and every poll_seconds (30) besides, starts each new job beside the ones running as the budget allows, and ends after one last look when nothing runs and nothing is queued. (2) pipeline.py nudge says that the queue changed, by touching a file in the state directory; sync.py commit runs it when its commit changed verification/jobs/ or priorities.json, in both modes, so whoever queues a job announces it without having to remember. (3) verification-loop.sh, waiting for work, looks at once after a nudge. (4) pipeline.py wait blocks until a job has finished and waits to be collected, or no runner is at work, and /run-verification now collects, triages and commits each result as it comes while the other jobs run. (5) watch.py wait, the watcher's loop, announces a job it sees queued that nobody announced (once), and starts a verification loop if none is running while jobs wait, unless the watcher stopped it; watch.py verification nudge does the first by hand.

Reading the queue had to become cheap for this: it took 6.4 s here, a git process or two for each of 407 job files, and now takes 0.3 s, with one git cat-file for all the files and a source commit looked up only for jobs still waiting. The runner writes its pid into its lock file, so that wait and nudge can tell a runner is at work without trying the lock, which would turn away a runner starting at that moment.

Verified by the default test run (46 of 47 on the first run; the one failure was a test listing a commit's exact steps, updated and rerun with its neighbours), with new tests: a job committed during a run starts at a nudge and its result is collected before the run ends; without a nudge the interval finds it; the verification loop starts a run at a nudge long before its interval (stand-ins for the pipeline and for claude); a commit that queues a job tells the pipeline and one that does not stays quiet; the watcher announces once and restarts a loop that is gone. The verification loop was restarted on the new script before this commit. Job 20261116-160826-the-pipeline-s-own-tests-run-by-the-pipe runs the pipeline's tests under the runner, and is also the first job announced by its own commit on the real queue.

commits.summary: Example 288 (CVE-2024-38820) set up from its catalog entry: locale-table decision claim and preservation frozen, replays pass
commits.body:
Example 288 was a catalog entry (revisions pinned, no tasks). It is now a deep negative packet, prepared as llm-dlc/runtime.md's catalog entry brief asks, with example 286 (CVE-2022-22968, the fix this one corrects) as the model. The release pair is Spring Framework 6.1.13 -> 6.1.14, from published JARs. Each release's DataBinder.java is the exact-fix pair's blob (c7af62b5, 98157756). Every other class the decision and the bind reach is byte-identical in the two closures. sources.lock.json records the tags, blobs, ancestry, JAR hashes against Maven Central, and a hand sweep of every JDK 21/25 locale: only tr and az lowercase an ASCII letter apart from the root locale, and only I.

There are two claims and six tasks. The decision claim is 286's assertion and ASCII domain, with the default locale as two int inputs indexing a table (root, en-US, tr-TR, az-AZ, lt-LT): one locale while the binder is configured, one while it decides. It says a field a disallowed pattern matches ignoring ASCII case is denied. It is expected refuted on 6.1.13, established on 6.1.14, and refuted on a mutant that lowercases the field in the default locale again. Preservation: outside the locale-dependent aliases (a capital I in the field decided under tr/az, or in a pattern configured under them), both releases decide alike. The controls are adapters, a driver, 36 probes and an independent oracle with a self-test.

The release pair is Spring Security 5.6.3 -> 5.6.4, from published JARs. Each release's RegexRequestMatcher.java is the exact-fix pair's blob (9264b56f, a334afc7). There are two claims and six tasks. The security claim covers a matcher built as RegexRequestMatcher(P + ".*", null, caseInsensitive), where P is a literal ASCII prefix.
