commits.summary: Example 289: a pattern that is an input is modelled where the own checker shows it is a literal followed by .*, and the four frozen claims are queued through the adapter entry (verification pending)
commits.body:
Example 289 is CVE-2022-22978 (Spring Security 5.6.3 to 5.6.4): RegexRequestMatcher compiled the rule it was given without Pattern.DOTALL, so /admin/.* did not match /admin/ followed by a line feed. Its two frozen claims quantify over the pattern (a literal prefix and .*), the case mode and every request String, so java.util.regex is on the proof's path with a pattern that is an input. The claims are unchanged.

The verifier's own checker (lib/src/bmc) gained one guarded rule and what the path needs beside it. regex.rs: Pattern.compile(String, int) of a String that is no constant is modelled only where the solver shows that on the path the String can only be characters that stand for themselves followed by .*; the Pattern is then those characters as a quoted text and . any number of times, and any other pattern stays the JDK's call, a gap refused by name. The flags CASE_INSENSITIVE and DOTALL are formulas (a constructor chooses them by an input, and paths that chose differently may have merged before the call); that no other flag is set is the solver's to show. One .* that ends an expression takes surrogates: what comes before it matched none, so it never begins inside a pair, and neither a pair nor a surrogate alone is a line terminator, so matching by unit is the JDK's matching by code point there; a dot anywhere else still makes an input with a surrogate the JDK's call. strings.rs: Character.isLetter of an ASCII char, the JDK's call of any other. runtime.rs: the java.util.logging levels below INFO as constants and Logger.isLoggable of one as false, under an assumption each outcome states (the matcher's debug line through spring-jcl is not written). models: IntStream.range(int, int) enters a model the checker runs (RangeStream), as String.chars() does.

Evidence for the rules: lib/tests/claims.rs has a new tool-tier test over a new fixture, claims.P. It proves the rule is its definition written out in Java (begins with the literal, ASCII case folded under CASE_INSENSITIVE, no line terminator after it without DOTALL) under each flag combination and with the flags chosen by an input, on every pattern and String of the bound; refutes a wrong claim on a witness run on a JVM; shows the refusals by name (any pattern, any text before the dot, another flag, a dot inside with a surrogate in the input, isLetter outside ASCII, isLoggable at INFO); and samples the definitions against the JDK on a JVM, with the five line terminators, surrogates alone and in pairs, the letters that fold outside ASCII, and isLetter on every char. lib/README.md and lib/models/README.md describe the rules.

The example: proofs/prove.py passes each frozen claim to jvmcontract through the adapter entry on the release's own bytecode, with no lemma and nothing put in a method's place, and builds the mutant by the replay route's recipe (the JAR it gives has the SHA-256 the mutant replay's receipt records). It follows loops for 26 turns where the default is 16: the allowed change reads a URL of up to 25 units, and at 16 the preservation check ended with no verdict, saying a loop was covered by an invariant. proofs/predicates.py compiles the claims' assumption, assertion and allowed change with javac and evaluates them on the 44 probes: they read each as controls/oracle.py does. target.json, example.json and the README record the queue, the probes and what became of the four predicted blockers.

Verified: inline probes at the frozen bound, each one capped run, gave every expected verdict (fixed-security established in 28 s, vulnerable-security and mutant-security refuted in 3 s each on witnesses run on a JVM, the mutant's with caseInsensitive true; preservation established in 47 s, and refuted at bound 3 with no allowed change). The unit tests (285) and the claims, values, pairing, conformance, loops, object_strings, string_literals, tiers and value_parameters tests pass; test_costs.py lint agrees; validate_example.py 289 passes. The default test run was not run: it is owed when the example is decided.

Jobs queued, the results of record: 20261116-214343-example-289-fixed-security-through-the-a, 20261116-214344-example-289-vulnerable-security-through, 20261116-214344-example-289-mutant-security-through-the, 20261116-214344-example-289-preservation-through-the-ada, and the proof tier after the engine changes, 20261116-214344-the-proof-tier-after-example-289-s-engin.

Also in this commit, collected by the pipeline's runner and found uncommitted in the working copy: the results of three of example 288's jobs. The proof tier after 288's engine changes passed (35m47s). 288's vulnerable-security and mutant-security ended on the checker's own 30-minute limit with no verdict, not with a wrong one; they are to be resubmitted larger in 288's next cycle, as its handoff says. commits.summary: Example 290: a library initializer the checker does not run is observed on a JVM, registrations are a LinkedHashMap in order and classes are found by name, and fixed-security is queued through the adapter entry (verification pending)
commits.body:
Example 290 (CVE-2023-34035, Spring Security 5.8.4 to 5.8.5: requestMatchers(String...) chooses a matcher type by the servlet context's registrations) gets its proof script, proofs/prove.py, which passes the frozen claims to jvmcontract through the adapter entry on the releases' own bytecode, beside the route, and proofs/predicates.py, which shows that the claims' expressions as javac compiles them agree with the oracle on the 27 select probes. An inline probe established fixed-security at the frozen bound of 8 in 6.9 s (659 paths). It is queued as job 20261116-225709-example-290-fixed-security-through-the-a. The two refutations and preservation are not decided: target.json's handoff says where each stops (Collections.emptyMap, Arrays.asList, ArrayList's addAll and toArray; then the matchers' constructors).

What the verifier gained for it (lib/). The new kind: prove --observed-initializer CLASS (src/observed.rs, src/bmc/observed.rs). Spring's ClassUtils builds its tables through an IdentityHashMap, a HashSet and a map of soft references, which the checker does not run (identity hash order, a float load factor, reference queues), and the servlet API's GenericServlet and HttpServlet each load a resource bundle. Such an initializer has no input, so the tool runs it on a JVM instead: the class is initialized in a JVM of its own, first thing, on the check's class path, its static fields are read by reflection, and the checker takes that state where a use initializes the class. Held: null, integral and boolean primitives, Strings (and whether each is the pooled one), Classes, a java.util.HashMap of String keys (as the HashMap model's entries) and arrays of those; any other value is not held, and a read of such a field is refused by name. A result that used one states it among what it rests on: one observation on the check's JDK, taken to be what the initializer leaves in every run. It is asked for class by class, is refused with --cache and for an initializer that throws, and is never used for the class under proof: the registry's own initializer runs as written. A class of a JDK package that the class path holds (javax.servlet's) is the JDK's to the checker, initialized already; naming it as observed is how its initializer is now accounted for.

Beside it: a model of java.util.LinkedHashMap for the checker alone (models/java/util/LinkedHashMap.java: the HashMap model's chain, which is in insertion order, with values(), its size and a fail-fast iterator); Arrays.stream(int[]) as a stream model; an int, short or byte in the compiler's concatenation as its decimal digits (String model 6; such a String had no content before); Class.forName(String) of a constant name with its initialization, and both forms of forName left to the JDK where a supertype is missing from the class path; Class.isAssignableFrom of two class literals; Thread.currentThread() and its context class loader as the class path's, under a stated assumption.

Verified by: lib/tests/claims.rs, two new tests over the new fixtures claims.M, claims.Tables, claims.Fails and javax.claims.Library (each model against its definition written out on every input of a bound; the observed state read as the JVM has it, an unheld field refused by name, the gap without the option, a throwing initializer and --cache refused), with claims.Samples running the same methods on a JVM; the unit tests (288 pass, three new in observed.rs); and the test files of the changed code (claims 14, values 18, conformance 10, loops, object_strings, pairing, string_literals, tiers, value_parameters). Two values tests that pinned the old behaviour were updated: a concatenated int now has content (a boolean is the gap that remains), and LinkedHashMap() is modelled (LinkedHashMap(Map) is the gap that remains). test_costs.py lint agrees; validate_example.py 290 passes. The default test run and the proof tier job follow once the example's remaining engine work is in.

commits.summary: The tests of a change are chosen from what it changed, the default run runs Rust beside Python and retries what fails once, and a failing default-run job traces each failure to its commit
commits.body: Four ways to make the default test run (about 16 minutes) less of a bottleneck. test_costs.py run --changed (--from REV for a line of commits) chooses statically from jj diff: a Python test file runs when it changed, when a module it imports transitively changed, or when its code, or a module it imports directly, names a changed file in a string (docstrings and records every module names, such as the trace index, job results and the inventory, don't count); cargo test runs when lib/ changed outside its Python tools and pages, only the changed binaries when only lib/tests/*.rs changed. run now starts cargo test beside the Python files (--serial for the old order), so the wall time is the longer half, not the sum. What fails is run once more, a Python file whole and Rust's failed tests by name; what passes then is reported FLAKY, counted as passed and named in the tally. The default-run job (verification/default_tests.py) streams its output, and on a failure halves the first-parent commits since the last passed run for each failing test, within 20 minutes, printing 'default tests: culprit TEST: COMMIT'; the watcher's default-tests event carries the culprits and the flaky tests. commits.body:
test_costs.py run: cargo only builds the Rust test binaries (--no-run), and they then run several at a time (--rust-jobs, by default half the CPUs, at most 4, and one per 1.5 GB of a job's memory limit), the longest first by what each took the last time (kept in the target directory). The Python test files run several at a time too (--python-jobs, 3 by default, 2 in a job); a file that fails has its second run alone after the others, so two files that disturbed each other show as flaky. The proof tier still runs one binary at a time, and --rust-jobs 1 --python-jobs 1 is the run as it was. Measured on this machine: the Rust binaries 707 s one after another in the first job, 403 s three at a time under a six-CPU limit beside another test job (peak 3.4 GB), 230 s four at a time; the whole default run 276 s, 49 of 49 passed, nothing flaky.

Three Rust test files prepare their fixtures together and not one after another, with the same assertions: observations.rs's Box Office examples test builds its ten patched examples four at a time (the binary went from 146 s to 71 s alone) and keeps the Gradle build between runs under a hash of its sources, tasks and JDK; application_core.rs and application_core_joint.rs compile their nineteen fixture builds four at a time.

default_tests.py: a run in the pipeline's fresh export records which files nothing opened and which folders nothing listed, from their access times (one packed line in its log; 'default_tests.py unread JOB' lists it), and a passed run then covers a later commit that only modifies those files or adds and removes files inside those folders. lib/ always counts as read, a rename is never covered, and a filesystem without access times records nothing. A probe of the Python half in an export left 546 entries unread, among them the example pages, CLAUDE.md and the runtime page. 'default_tests.py flaky' counts flaky tests over the collected runs. sync.py adopt-logs takes a log as a hard link where it can. Verified by the default run above, which includes the new tests of each piece (stand-in cargo and made-up runs); the inventory has the eight new Python rows, added by hand as the handoff note says.

commits.summary: /run-brief: a watcher runs a feature brief on command, with a foundation stage on Fable 5.2 before its streams
commits.body:
A brief of llm-dlc/loops/ was started by hand, and its run was known to run-streams.sh only through a list of five names in the script. A local skill, /run-brief (.claude/skills/run-brief, not part of the plugin), now runs any brief with a watcher session on Opus 5.5, as /prove-java-change runs a proof. Its tool is llm-dlc/tools/brief_run.py: a preflight that finds what run-streams.sh would stop at before anything starts and says what the verification runner may keep beside this many loops (budget --apply lowers verification/pipeline.local.toml for the run); a foundation stage, one Fable 5.2 session at high effort given the user's instruction to start the work itself, build the foundation it sees fit and update the brief for the agents that take over, in a workspace of its own so no other session's uncommitted files meet its commits; land, which brings its commits to the default line, moved forward or by a merge with the generated trace files regenerated, and takes back a merge that conflicts in real work; start, which runs run-streams.sh detached; and wait, which returns only what needs the watcher (a blocked loop, a failing integration check, an open decision, a missing verification loop, a summary every 30 minutes, the end).

run-streams.sh takes a brief by name or file and reads its streams from the brief's Loop settings (- streams: a, b); the five older briefs keep their lists, a brief with no streams runs as its own loop, --plan prints what was read, and a stream brief's fork is optional. With a watcher, a loop that ends blocked is put to it (conductor.py's new blocked question: rerun or leave, half an hour at most), so a decision reaches its stream during the run instead of after it; the verdict is a decision in the record. A stream waiting on jobs is checked every minute, not every five. The brief template gains the streams setting, how a brief is run, and an opt-in test policy (tests: queued: the default run as a job per commit instead of a wait before each next piece), which CLAUDE.md names as an exception for such a brief's own loops.

Verified by llm-dlc/tools/test_brief_run.py (24 tests on a made-up jj repository with stand-ins for claude, feature-loop.sh and sync.py, including run-streams.sh end to end: a blocked stream run again at the watcher's word, one left without an answer, a brief with no streams, and a run started and watched by the tool) and by the default test run, 49 of 49 files. No brief has been run through it with real sessions. Not built from the user's plan (~/docs/01-feature-stream-plumbing-plan.md): the result collector in a workspace of its own, the submitted, released and accepted boundary, a submission boundary in feature-loop.sh, routing inside wait, early merge and a headless watcher. The work is in the jj workspace run-brief, beside the default line, which a proof run is using.

The user wants to start a brief's run from a session that is already open, which then is the watcher. The skill says so: any Opus 5.5 session of the default workspace can be asked in words, the run's state is all in files, and a new section, A run under way, has the watcher read brief_run.py status first and either go straight to waiting (a run it takes over), continue an interrupted run, or start a new one.

Two gaps in the preflight, found by checking it against the proof run under way: feature-loop.sh runs from a private copy of itself, so looking for prove-loop.sh by name missed a running proof loop, and the preflight now blocks on any feature loop at work in the default workspace; and a brief without a session setting falls back on the loops' one default session, so each brief of the run must name a session and no two the same.

Verified by test_brief_run.py, 26 tests, and the cost-tier lint. The whole default run was not repeated: it passed 49 of 49 on the commit before, and only brief_run.py, its tests, the skill and the README changed since.

commits.summary: /run-brief: a commit takes only its own files, a run stops at a boundary, the foundation's report reaches each stream's inbox, and a summary says where the time went
commits.body:
Four additions the user chose before the first run of a brief through its watcher. (1) sync.py commit --only PATH ... commits the named files and folders alone: every other file changed in the working copy is set aside in a change below, and put back uncommitted after the commit, so the files on disk never change. The result collector commits with the paths pipeline.py commit-paths names (verification/, the examples table, the outputs it applied), and the loops' instruction names --only in place of a procedure to follow by hand; on 2026-11-16 a commit of results took a watcher's unfinished merge with it. A collector in a workspace of its own was the plan's wording and is not what this does: every reader of results reads them on the default line, so its commits would have to be landed there one by one, which brings the shared working copy back. (2) brief_run.py stop NAME stops a run at a boundary: run-streams.sh gives each loop a directory for command lines, each running loop is told to end after its cycle, a loop waiting on jobs stops waiting, nothing is run again and the merge is not started; start continues, and stop --now interrupts as before. (3) Landing the foundation puts its closing report into each stream's inbox as an item of a new kind, foundation, which the stream acknowledges. (4) run-streams.sh logs each change of a loop's phase with its time, and a summary says per loop how long it worked, waited on jobs, was blocked, and sat finished while another stream still ran.

Verified by test_commit_only.py on a real jj repository (the named paths committed, a modified, an added and a nested file of another session left uncommitted with their contents), test_brief_run.py (28 tests: a run stopped while a stream waits on jobs, then continued to its merge; the hand-off sent once; the time lines), and test_costs.py run --changed, 26 of 27 files, the one failure an assertion of mine on the order two parallel streams start in, since fixed and run three times. Telling a real loop to end after its cycle is the command path the proof loop's watcher already uses, and is not exercised here with a real session. The working copy went stale during this work and was restored from a backup, compared against jj's own snapshot.

commits.body:
The user went through ten gaps of /run-brief one by one. What they chose is built here. A workspace jj calls stale is put right by llm-dlc/tools/unstale.py, which CLAUDE.md now names: it saves the files changed since jj last looked, runs jj workspace update-stale, takes the edits back from the second copy of the working-copy change that jj leaves (only the files that copy changed), and abandons the copy; a second copy without staleness, which two operations at once also leave, is abandoned when the working copy holds all it has. While the foundation session runs, brief_run.py wait tells the watcher at each interval how long it has run, its tool calls, the command under way and its last commit; no cap was wanted. A loop that ends blocked is run again at the watcher's word twice at most in a run (RUN_STREAMS_RERUNS), then left without a question. Landing the foundation by a merge puts back, uncommitted, whatever another session wrote into the working copy while the merge was made. The foundation's spend is in the summary and its total, and brief_run.py verification start|stop records the verification loop with the brief's run, so the watcher can stop the one it started. Left as they are, by the user's choice: the wait of 30 minutes for an answer about a blocked loop, and a runner that keeps its budget until its run ends (they plan to rework the pipeline). The collector keeps commit --only in place of a workspace of its own.

The user decided to take the default run out of the verification pipeline: as a job it overlapped other runs in one cargo target directory (VF-034), was cut off with its runner at the Bash tool's 10-minute limit, and skipped the one-at-a-time lock when queued from a line that predated it. verification/default_tests.py (queue, step, supersede, bisect, the unread-file list, flaky counts) and its tests are removed, with verification/default-tests-unread.txt and the watcher's default-tests event.

commits.summary: The watcher of a brief's run merges each stream the moment it is finished; there is no merge loop
commits.body: At the user's word after the first /run-brief rehearsal (2026-11-17), whose merge loop took the finished streams for empty because their notes were not in its working copy's files, and in which a finished stream waited for the slowest. run-streams.sh now puts each finished stream, done or left blocked, to the watcher at once (conductor.py's new merge question, RUN_STREAMS_MERGE_WAIT, 30 min), while the others still run, and no longer runs the brief's own loop after the streams; a brief without streams still runs as its own loop, now labelled brief. brief_run.py merge BRIEF STREAM merges the stream's @- into the default line as land does, takes its session logs (land now runs sync.py adopt-logs too) and inbox acknowledgements, answers the question merged, records the merge in the brief's Progress (status done once every stream is merged and done, blocked: stream S: ... when one was left blocked) and commits it with the decision; it commits the run's own decision record first, so the watcher's earlier answers don't block it, and run again after a hand-made merge it only records it. Without a watcher nothing is merged and the run's end names the command. conductor.py numbers events under a lock: two streams finishing in the same second both took event 1 and each other's verdict. The skill, llm-dlc/README.md, the brief template, stream-conductor.md's Design 5 and the rehearsal brief (no index.md any more, fresh session ids) say so. Verified with test_costs.py run --changed: 8 test files, 194 tests, all passed, among them new end-to-end tests in test_brief_run.py (both streams merged by the watcher as they finish, the brief done, nothing uncommitted, a second merge recording nothing; a blocked stream merged and named in the status; no watcher, no merge) and a test in test_conductor.py that fails without the lock.

commits.summary: The watcher of a brief's run collects and commits verification results itself, and landing drops trace output left uncommitted
commits.body:
With a watcher, run-streams.sh starts no verification loop. At each look at the queue, brief_run.py wait collects the results that are back and commits them with --only the paths pipeline.py commit-paths names, starts the runner (pipeline.py run, no model) when jobs wait and none is at work, and records the inbox items the streams' committed Progress acknowledges. It returns a 'results' event with the jobs to triage in 'attention'; the watcher triages them as the run-verification skill says. brief_run.py collect does the same by hand, for the report. A verification loop already running keeps the queue as before. Merges and collections take turns by a lock, so the watcher is the one session committing in the default working copy while a run is under way.

land (and so merge) now treats uncommitted trace output (llm-dlc/traces/, llm-dlc/index.json, the decision views, and llm-dlc/README.md when only its session table changed) as nobody's work: it is dropped, not waited for and not carried onto the other line, and the next sync.py run writes it again. In the rehearsal it was there after the foundation landed, and a second real-time merge would have waited for a commit no session was going to make. A move forward that makes another session's uncommitted files conflict is taken back; the jj steps hold sync.py's repository lock; the precise list of generated paths replaces the 'llm-dlc/ or README.md' prefix that sent any file under llm-dlc/ written during a merge into the merge commit.

commits.summary: A proof by induction and a lemma's summary no longer stand in for a call that writes, throws, or reads what a caller can change
commits.body:
Three false proofs, each reproduced first on the checker as it was (lib/tests/fixtures/claims/claims/Effects.java, whose main prints what a JVM says): (1) prove --decreases on a method that counts its calls in a static field proved 'result == 1' where a JVM returns 2, because the induction hypothesis replaced the inner call and dropped its write; (2) with a throws clause, the hypothesis returned a value for an inner call the property itself says throws, and proved 'result == n' of a method that never returns; (3) a lemma about a getter, proved in the fresh state where its static field is 0, was used as a summary after the caller wrote the field, and proved 'result == 0' of a method that returns what it wrote. The same held through a callee, through an array a static field holds, for the default locale, and for a lemma whose own assertion reads a field.

Now: a method proved by induction is held to the write checks a summary's method already had (Options::own_induction says the proof is by induction alone, where reads are sound because the inner calls are made in the state of the call under proof); the hypothesis does not cover arguments on which a throws clause says the call throws (the induction then does not go through); a lemma's method, and the lemma's assumption and assertion, may read no static field that is not final, no non-final field or cell of an object that was there before the call, and not the default locale (Engine::reads); a summary is not used while its method's class is still being initialized. A lemma about a method of no parameters now compiles (its assertion is over the result alone).

Which existing results rest on these mechanisms: none uses prove --decreases directly; examples 286 and 288 use lemmas about PatternMatchUtils.simpleMatch(String,String), whose bytecode in the pinned 5.3.19 JAR reads no field and no array (javap), so their results did not rest on the hole; that the tightened checks still prove those lemmas is for a job to confirm. Verified by lib/tests/claims.rs (18 passed, among them the three new tests and the changed lemma test: a method that counts with calls++ is now refused at its read, one that only writes at its write), the summary unit tests, and test_costs.py run --changed (8 of 8 passed: cargo test's 33 binaries and three Python files).

commits.summary: An answer given beside the route counts only when what its job left gives it: the acceptance check (verification pending)
commits.body:
Until now llm-dlc/tools/changes.py counted a task's besideRoute answer when its job had passed and named the example. That says a script exited 0: one passed job supported either answer, example 290's one job confirmed four, and a trial run at a smaller bound was told from the full claim by nothing. examples/tools/accept.py now derives the answer from the evidence and accepts the recorded one only when every check holds (its first lines list them): the job's result and the job file it is of; the step that ran the example's driver on this task; the outcome that step wrote, among the collected outputs with the bytes the result records; the outcome's own verdict; the claim file as frozen and as the job ran it at its source commit; the task, the pinned artifacts and the adapter sources as they were then; the outcome's assumption, assertion and throws clauses, and a preservation task's allowed change; the entry; the bound (a proof at a smaller bound establishes nothing, a witness found at one refutes when it lies in the claim's domain); the engine and gap mode; for an establishment, complete bounds and an input that reaches the property; for a refutation, a witness reproduced on a JVM; for a constructed mutant, that its JAR is the one the mutant replay ran. changes.py uses it, and says which check refuses an answer.

On the saved results: example 289's four answers and 290's four are accepted, as an outside review found by hand for 289 on 2026-11-16. Examples 286's and 287's mutant-security are not: their drivers neither print nor record the mutant JAR's hash, so nothing says it was the JAR the mutant replay ran; changes.py lists both claims as open again (both examples were already 'prepared', so no example changes state), and their notes say what closes it. Every accepted answer carries one limit, that the jobs recorded no identity of the JARs, the compiled adapter or the verifier's binary. Example 289's driver now writes evidence.json beside its outcome with those (accept.record), ends the run when the mutant's JAR is not the replay's (it only printed both hashes), and marks a run at another bound a trial; one capped inline probe of its shortest task (vulnerable-security, 5 s) showed the record written and the verdict unchanged.

Two jobs are queued. 20261117-122454-example-289-the-four-proof-tasks-again-w reruns 289's four tasks with the recording driver into verification/.work-289/recorded, so the earlier jobs' outputs stay as their results record them; the tasks' besideRoute still name the earlier jobs until it has passed. 20261117-122546-examples-286-and-288-the-simplematch-lem reruns fixed-security of 286 and 288 on the checker after the lemma checks of the commit before last were tightened, to confirm the simpleMatch lemma is still proved (its bytecode reads no field and no array).

Verified by examples/tools/test_accept.py (28 tests: the controls for a wrong conclusion, a missing result, a changed artifact and a trial bound, the driver's record, and this checkout's own example 289), llm-dlc/tools/test_changes.py (22, with the answer a job's outcome contradicts), validate_example.py 289, and test_costs.py run --changed: 38 of 38 passed (cargo test and 37 Python files).

commits.summary: The verification runner reads the machine's settings from ~/.config/in-the-loop, so a side workspace judges jobs by this machine's limits
commits.body: verification/pipeline.local.toml is gitignored, so it existed only in the default workspace, and submit in any other jj workspace judged a job by the committed defaults, a laptop's (4 GB a job): an agent in a side workspace was told the local runner could not run a 6 GB job that the runner here, at 24 GB a job, would take. load_config now reads, in order, pipeline.toml, the machine's file (~/.config/in-the-loop/pipeline.local.toml; XDG_CONFIG_HOME moves it, VERIFY_MACHINE_CONFIG names another or none), the checkout's own pipeline.local.toml, VERIFY_CONFIG, then flags. submit's 'cannot run' note names the settings it judged by, and says when they were the committed defaults alone. brief_run.py budget edits whichever file gives the runner its budget: the checkout's when it sets one, else the machine's. Every test run (test_costs.py run) and test_pipeline set VERIFY_MACHINE_CONFIG empty, so no test reads this machine's settings: without it two pipeline tests failed with a machine file in place. commits.summary: A write set, a first effect contract: prove --writes refutes the setter that writes a protected field and proves its honest twin
commits.body: The state stream's steps 4 and 5, the checking side. prove --writes this.displayName (own checker only) states which fields of a method's receiver and object parameters it may write. The check proves the frame with the property: after a normal return every other field of those inputs is unchanged, a primitive by value and a String or object by identity through the new p == \old(p) term. The frame is conjoined to the assertion, so a write outside the set is refuted by the harness and its witness runs on a JVM. Inside the call the engine refuses, by name, a write to anything else that existed before it: a static field, an array, an object no input is (even one a named field holds), or a class initialization, whose objects would look new to the call. This generalizes Engine::keeps through bmc::Options::frame. The cache refuses such a check, since its key does not read the write set.

commits.summary: An effect contract at a call: a setter's checked write set stands in for its calls, and the application-level rename statement is proved through the honest setter and refuted through the adversarial one
commits.body:
A lemma with a writes: line is now an effect contract of a public instance method (prove --lemmas). It is proved first with its frame (the write set of the last commit) and also as reading nothing that was there before the call: no field of the receiver or an object argument, no static field that is not final, no array, no default locale, and no identity comparison of such an object (bmc::Options::closed_frame, which generalizes Engine::reads and Engine::compares as the write set generalized Engine::keeps). What the method writes is then a function of its arguments. In the check, a call on a receiver of exactly the contract's class, with arguments within its bounds, runs a stub of the claim's class (bmc::Effect, the effect intrinsic). A written field takes the parameter the assertion gives it (this.f == p; the expression language now compares a String field with a String parameter by identity), another written primitive takes any value, and nothing else changes. Elsewhere the method runs as written. A written reference field with no parameter, assume:, throws:, array parameters and non-integral results are refused by name.

Verified with lib/tests/fixtures/claims Frames: the honest setter's contract is proved and used (the statement lists it among what the run rests on), and 'an admin stays one under the new name' is proved. The adversarial setter's contract is refuted, so the check that rests on it is refused. Without it, 'a rename makes no account an admin' is refuted by a rename to admin:, and the witness replays. Five use-side countermodels each grant admin on a JVM (Frames.main): a name past the contract's bound, a receiver field a caller set, a static switch, a literal's identity, a subclass hook called through the inherited setter. Each was a false proof with its rule switched off (by mutation: closed_frame off, the exact-class check off, the stub's bounds guard off). New tests: two tool tests in claims.rs and unit tests for the stub, the conjunct split and String identity; test_costs run --changed passes and lint agrees. Inbox item domain-advances-state-I003 is taken in Progress. The brief is not wrong.

commits.summary: A write set's frame holds on a declared exceptional exit and is of locations over inputs that may be one object: the challenge stream's three false frames are refuted or proved as JML's assignable states them
commits.body:
Inbox item domain-advances-state-I005 (the challenge stream's countermodels, synvlnls, fc.Framed). Before this commit, prove --writes proved a frame in two cases where a JVM sees the protected field written. In the first, a method writes admin and then throws an exception its throws clause declares: the frame was part of the assertion, which was read only after a normal return. The harness now checks the frame after the expected exception too (harness::generate_property_framed, whose \old reads take their own locals after the assertion's), so rename("b", -1) is refuted with a witness a JVM replays. In the second, one bean is passed as two inputs. The frame is now of locations, as JML's assignable is. Every two inputs of one class may be one object: the check adds the alias choice, and the domain says so. A field that one of them names is framed in the other only where the two differ (this == other || this.admin == \old(this.admin)). So promote --writes other.admin and grant --writes to.admin are proved with that frame, which a JVM keeps, and never with the unaliased one, which it breaks. A write set with a construction plan over two inputs of one class is refused by name. Where a witness throws a declared exception over objects, its expected line now names the frame instead of wrongly saying 'a normal return'.

Tests. lib/tests/fixtures/frame-countermodels (README and fc/Framed.java) and the JVM test in lib/tests/frame_countermodels.rs are copied unchanged from synvlnls. The README's checker-side test a_write_set_is_not_proved_where_a_jvm_sees_a_field_it_does_not_name_written is added, adapted to the location frame: rename must be refuted with a JVM replay, and promote and grant must not prove the unaliased frame. The README's version required those two not to be Verified, which none of the options it lists for aliasing (a location frame, or distinct objects in the domain) would give. A second test proves that what the frame names is allowed on either exit and alias. My own countermodel claims.Frames$Linking#link writes its own name only where other is itself, and claims.rs requires it refuted with a JVM replay. Switching off each fix (by mutation) makes a test fail: the exit frame fails the README test, and the alias pairs fail the Linking case. test_costs run --changed: 35 cargo binaries and 5 of 5 default-tier checks pass; estimate, tag and lint agree.

Merge note: lib/tests/frame_countermodels.rs and the fixture are added on both this line and the challenge line, so a merge conflicts on the test file (take this line's). An effect contract (vwktulky) is proved through the same check, so its stub's writes now rest on a frame of locations that holds on every exit the contract allows. commits.body:
Example 286's protected-state path (state stream, step 3). The evidence stream's binding of an observed initializer to what it was observed on (lzpqszyo) is copied onto this line unchanged: lib/src/observed.rs, lib/src/observed/ObservedInitializer.java, lib/src/classpath.rs (ClassPath::refused, from mqkqvvmw), lib/tests/observed_countermodels.rs with its fixtures, and lib/README.md's paragraph. With the binding, 286's probe (fixed-protected-state-mutation at bound 2, a trial) ended before DataBinder.bind. Initializing CachedIntrospectionResults initializes ReflectionUtils, and the binding compares that class's state with its state when initialized alone. It found USER_DECLARED_METHODS to be 'an object of ReflectionUtils$$Lambda/0x000000006604a6e8' in one run and '...$$Lambda/0x000000000e040a90' in the other, and refused the observation as a write to another class. The address is the JVM's name for the lambda's hidden class, and it differs from run to run. The observer now names a hidden class by what it was defined from (R$$Lambda), both for an object it does not hold and for a HashMap key's class. commits.summary: A library method the own checker can't run may be replaced by a stand-in sampled against it on a JVM (prove --stand-in), and a result that used one says it rests on it
commits.body:
Step 3, option 2, of the state stream's brief. Spring's bean wrapper resolves a property through its introspection caches and java.beans and calls the setter with Method.invoke, on every path of DataBinder.bind (example 286). Observing those caches is refused, and running them would need models of java.beans and java.lang.reflect. So the binding path gets a stand-in instead. Each public static method of the stand-in class (but main) replaces an instance method: its first parameter's class is the exact class of the receivers it covers, the rest of its descriptor is the method's. A call resolving to that method on a receiver of exactly that class runs the stand-in. A subclass's receiver, and the stand-in's own calls, run the method as written, so a stand-in hands back what it does not cover. Its main prints one line per sample with the method's outcome and the stand-in's. The tool runs it first on the check's class path and takes the stand-in only if every sample is the same, refusing it by the first input that differs, or when nothing is sampled, or for a public method that replaces nothing. A result that used a stand-in names it among what it rests on, with the number of samples, as sampled evidence and not a proof. A refutation through one is still replayed on a JVM. JBMC and --cache are refused.

Verified by lib/tests/stand_in.rs on the fixture lib/tests/fixtures/stand-ins, a reflective property writer. With the stand-in, a claim the method leaves undecided is proved and the stand-in is named; a refutation replays on a JVM. A subclass receiver, and a bean the stand-in hands back, stop at the method's gap as before. A stand-in that forgets 'Age', one that samples nothing, and one with a public helper are refused. Switching off the exact-receiver check, or the sample comparison, by mutation makes a test fail. test_costs run --changed passes, after the proof cache's projection named the new option. 286's own stand-in is drafted, not committed: sampled against 5.3.19's setPropertyValue, its 38,400 samples all match. Two countermodels of the pair (lib/src/pairing.rs) were each proved to agree though a caller tells the versions apart. The fix has two parts. First, the scope meantToChange was called on the caller's own arrays, and the versions' copies were taken after it, so a scope that zeroed a cell decided what both versions saw; it is now called on copies of its own. Second, an exception was compared by its class's name alone; it is now compared by that name and the names of every class above it up to Object, by a recursive same(ea, eb) over Class.getSuperclass(). The tool's own checker now names those bits by the state the loop is summarized from (lib/src/bmc/ties.rs, wired into bmc/loops.rs and bmc/mod.rs, with shared::fingerprint comparing the code). A summary of the same code from the same state, on either side, takes the same bits, and a read past such a loop at an index the path does not follow is named by the array's content and the index. The key is everything an iteration can read: the code with everything it reaches, the head, the live locals, the objects reachable from them and from the static fields that code uses (numbered as reached, so an alias is part of it), the JDK's statics and the classes' initialization. Only values are shared; each side leaves the loop by its own code. This is step 2's boundary, chosen over the unchanged callee as one function (which would have to carry crypt_raw's effects across heaps) and a coupled invariant; the brief's Progress says why.

Countermodels first (lib/tests/pairing.rs, seven variants of one table-mixing loop): a callee changed inside the loop, a cell, an alias on one side, a mutable static, a shorter array and a write past the loop on one side each differ on a JVM and are not proved, and five of them were Verified with their side condition taken out (checked by hand with a switch since removed). A capped probe of 287 at bound 80: the new release's summaries of ekskey and crypt_raw take the previous release's bits and the spurious counterexample is gone; the check then reaches the key schedule and stops at the 240 s limit, mostly in crypt_raw's rounds loop's invariant search (287's notes). test_costs.py run --changed passes; validate_example.py 287 passes.

commits.summary: The checker takes bcrypt's crypt_raw as one function of both releases: a call on a receiver nothing reads after it, returning an array it makes; 287's preservation verifies in a capped probe at bound 80 (verification pending)
commits.body:
Example 287's preservation claim compares Spring Security 6.3.7 and 6.3.8 on BCryptPasswordEncoder.matches. Two jobs related the two releases at bcrypt's loop summaries and stopped undecided at the previous release's BCrypt.key loop. This moves the relation up to the call of crypt_raw, whose nine methods are the same bytecode in both releases, as the 307 specialist's prototype and an outside review suggested (inbox items I015 and I018).

The rule for a call both versions share (lib/src/bmc/ties.rs, lib/src/shared.rs one_function) now takes three more cases. An instance method, where nothing can read its receiver after the call: no live local of any frame (an exception's handler counted), no other stack place, no static field, no other object; the receiver's fields are among the inputs. An array result, where the code returns an array it made of a length it computes from constants and static tables' lengths that is a constant at the call (crypt_raw's new byte[cdata.length * 4]). An array whose cells hold any values, as an input named by its content. What a call may write is what it reaches through an argument, the receiver, or a static its code takes other than to copy it at once, so bcrypt's tables, which it only clones, stay inputs. Two cost fixes found by profiling: inputs that are the same formulas are now related without a solver literal, and a check whose first run used the whole budget reports that run rather than an empty fallback.

Countermodels first: KEYED in lib/tests/pairing.rs (the receiver read after the call through a live local, a static or a handler; another field value on each side; an argument returned in place of a made array; a static table the call writes). Each differs on a JVM and is not proved. With each side condition switched off in turn (a temporary switch, removed), exactly its own rows were proved. lib/tests/fixtures/callee-countermodels on JDK 25 (check.py --rule-landed) still proves no countermodel, with same, copied and parsed verified. Capped probes at the frozen bounds: 287 preservation verified in 112 s (53 paths, 52 calls taken as one function); 307 preservation verified and its mutant refuted; 289 and 290 verify as before. test_costs.py run --changed passes (26 of 26) and validate_example.py 287 passes. The matcher takes under 3 s. Trial bounds show steep growth: verified in 13 s at 3 and 42 s at 4, undecided after 150 s at 5 and 6. It is relational: a disallowed pattern with a capital I configured under tr-TR that matches the field in no case lies outside the allowed change, yet the releases lower-case it apart. At bound 4 it related 154 of 309 applications and saved nothing, because the hard case has unequal inputs. The next approach, a lemma per release that a match of lower-cased Strings implies a match ignoring ASCII case, is in 288's notes. No job was queued: at the frozen bound one would repeat VF-031. commits.summary: /single-agent-run: one agent toward one outcome, with a watcher that judges after each cycle and can change what the next one is told
commits.body:
A third kind of watched run, beside /prove-java-change and /run-brief, for a goal well within one agent's reach, where a brief with streams is more than the work needs. The command takes a starting prompt, an optional brief file and a continue message. The first cycle is given the prompt, and every later one the run's continue message as it stands when that cycle starts, so the user can have the watcher change it between two cycles and steer a run that is under way. Both texts reach the agent word for word; a brief adds one sentence after each that names the file. After every cycle (one context window: the loop compacts the session after each) the watcher is given the agent's report, the cycle's commits, what it left uncommitted and the queue, and answers continue or stop; each answer is a decision in llm-dlc/decisions/single-NAME.jsonl.

The loop is a new mode of feature-loop.sh, single-agent, so a run has what every loop has: the memory cap, the record the loop statistics read, the session's own compaction at 600k tokens put to the watcher when no commit came, the closing summary, a count of cycles that can be changed while it runs. It differs from the other loops in one rule: a cycle with no commit does not stop it, because the watcher reads what that means (the outcome reached, a question, or stuck). Without a verdict in time (15 minutes, --verdict-wait) a cycle that committed is followed by another, one that did not ends the run before its compact as in every loop, and three in a row without a verdict end it, since nothing else measures such a run. llm-dlc/tools/single_run.py is the watcher's tool: start (in the checkout or in a jj workspace of its own, a new session, a continued one or a fork), wait, answer, message, status, summary, cycles, stop, jobs (for a run stopped only to wait on verification jobs), collect and land. It keeps the verification queue as a brief's watcher does, through brief_run.py's own functions, unless another run's watcher keeps it. The skill is .claude/skills/single-agent-run; llm-dlc/README.md has a section on it.

Also fixed in feature-loop.sh, for every loop: a stop that reached the loop before a cycle began (typed, or left by a watcher, before the first cycle or between the last look and the next cycle) was counted as a cycle to start, which left the count below zero, and nothing ended the loop. It now ends there. loop_stats.py reads the new record (every text such a run sent is a cycle, a cycle with no commit does not take the decision after it for the last commit's, and the watcher's own words for an ending are not matched against the other endings).

Verified with llm-dlc/tools/test_single_run.py (13 tests: the loop run for real in a made-up jj repository with a stand-in claude, through each of the above, a workspace made and landed, a fork, a stop and a restart included), and test_costs.py run --changed: 16 of 16 files passed, test_prove_loop.py (30) and test_brief_run.py (39) among them. No real session was started: the first run is the user's.

commits.summary: A single-agent run's continue message is a person's alone: the watcher can no longer set it
commits.body:
The user's decision on 2026-11-18, after reading the first version: the continue message is an option for a person to steer the session, given with an expert's review and written to account for a long run, and the watcher is never to modify it; the loop ending is preferred to a watcher steering, in almost all cases. The first version let the watcher set the message when the user asked, with an answer or by the message command.

Now single_run.py message sets the message only for a person at their own terminal (stdin and stdout a terminal and no CLAUDECODE in the environment, the test sync.py uses for its approvals) and is refused from a session with words that say what to do instead: end the run and say why. The answer command takes no message any more, and start refuses --continue on a run that already exists, so a restart cannot change it either. Printing the message and its history stays open to all. The question a watcher is given after a cycle says the message is never its to change and that stop is the answer when the run should not go on as it reads. The skill tells the watcher not to set it, edit its file, draft a replacement unasked, or get a new text to the agent another way, and to answer stop when the next cycle would need to be told something the message does not say; if the user asks it for a change, it gives them the command to run themselves. The README section says the same.

Verified with test_single_run.py (13 tests; the changed one shows the refusal from a session, a person's change taken by the next cycle and recorded as theirs, an answer that carries no message, and a restart that cannot change it) and test_costs.py run --changed: 16 of 16 files passed. In an earlier of the two runs of that command test_prove_loop.py failed once and passed when run again, with the machine at a load of 23 to 29 from the brief run under way; alone it passed three times in a row, and its tests wait one second for a verdict, which a loaded machine can miss. Which test it was is not known: the first run's output was not kept.

commits.summary: A brief's watcher gets a merge order and early merges, a stream's rerun, helpers, and a default test run only when it is due
commits.body:
What the domain-advances run (2026-11-17) showed the /run-brief watcher could not do, from an agent's analysis of that run and the user's notes on it. Seven of its ten points are built here; three are left out at the user's word (help deciding when to stop, the stale cost in summaries, and cleaning up workspaces at the end, which could lose data).

Merges that interact. `brief_run.py trial BRIEF` merges every pair of the streams' lines, and each with the default line, beside every working copy (`jj new --no-edit`, read, abandoned) and lists the files each pair conflicts in beyond the generated ones and the test inventory. `brief_run.py order BRIEF STREAM ...` records a merge order: `merge` refuses a stream while one before it has commits the line lacks, and the held-back stream's merge question names what to merge first. `merge BRIEF STREAM --early` merges a stream that is still at work as far as it has committed, leaving its uncommitted files, its question and the brief's status alone. In that run two streams conflicted in one file and the stream held back was answered `leave` for four hours.

A stream whose loop died (VF-037). `brief_run.py rerun BRIEF STREAM` leaves a request that run-streams.sh takes once the stream's own process has ended: the loop starts again inside the run, with its counts at nought, and is put to the watcher to merge when finished; after the run has ended the same command starts it again for that stream. Before any loop starts, run-streams.sh stops a scope that holds only what an ended loop left (the tests a session killed for memory was running), which is what made the restart fail and count as the stream's second failure; a scope with a loop at work in it is left alone.

Helpers. The user names a Claude Code session they have open, by its tmux pane (`/run-brief --helper "tmux 3"`, or later in words); the first is for low-hanging work and others may be added with a role of their own. `brief_run.py helper BRIEF add|task|done|merge|list`: a task is the watcher's text wrapped in a stream's standing rules, the helper's workspace is put at the default line's one last commit (never from a merge in progress), one line naming the task's file is typed into the pane (never into a pane at a shell prompt), the helper reports with `done`, `wait` returns it, and the watcher merges it. The skill also says how material from outside the run comes in (new files only, merged by the watcher, acknowledged through an inbox item of the new kind `delivered`) and when to suggest a specialist (the same wall for two cycles).

Who commits what. `wait` now commits the run's decision record whenever it has changed, the user's answers with the watcher's, under a message that says so (a user's answer had gone into a commit of results under that commit's message); the skill says to record an action only after it happened. feature-loop.sh drops its own and the run's variables before it starts `claude`, so a stream's test of these scripts can no longer put made-up questions to the real watcher, and the preflight refuses a watcher whose own environment carries a run's variables.

Tests. A change to lib/tests/costs.json no longer chooses any test in `test_costs.py run --changed` (it ran all of cargo test, which filled a stream's memory in VF-037), and a change to test_costs.py or cost_tier.py chooses the one Rust binary that reads them, `tiers`, not all of them. `default_run.py after-merge` runs the default test run after a merge only when the last one in the checkout failed or none passed there within the hour, and with `--final` whenever no passed run covers the commit, in a memory cap of its own (8G) with two Rust test binaries at a time. CLAUDE.md's Tests section, lib/README.md and both watcher skills say to use it after a merge: the user asked for the default run to be run less, and never because of the inventory.

Verified by 16 new tests (trial merges, the order, early merges, reruns inside and after a run, the scope cleared, helpers, the environment check, the due check) and: the tests of what changed passed, 25 of 25 (python3 lib/tools/test_costs.py run --changed --rust-jobs 1 under an 8G cap: the tiers binary of cargo test and 24 Python test files, among them all 50 tests of test_brief_run.py and the 13 of test_single_run.py), and the inventory's lint agrees. No real run has used any of this yet; the first /run-brief after the merge is the first end-to-end check. Nothing here is merged into the default line, where the domain-advances run's watcher is still at work.

commits.summary: A loop's session can be carried by Codex: one client boundary, models resolved at launch, the same instructions and skills for both clients
commits.body:
Brief 00 ("Run Codex and Claude Code from the same loop instructions", the user's, 2026-11-18): give the operator a choice of Codex or Claude Code for a loop's worker, with the briefs, the instruction of a cycle, the commit check, the conductor, the queue and the record unchanged. This is the worker's side of it, built on the current loops and not on the 2026-11-16 proof of concept's copies, whose findings it reuses.

The boundary is one file, llm-dlc/tools/agent_client.py. It starts a Codex turn (`codex exec --json`), resumes the session's own thread (`codex exec resume THREAD`), and prints the stream the loops already read from Claude Code (init, assistant text and tool calls, compact_boundary, one closing result), so the progress display, the compaction watch, a cycle's report and the cost accounting keep their one reader; Claude Code's turns are started as before, argument for argument. A loop names its session by a UUID and Codex names its thread itself: the binding is written whole when Codex reports the thread, a later turn resumes exactly that thread, and a client that reports another ends the turn as an error. Each attempt keeps Codex's events, its stderr, its last message and a digest of what it was given. Compaction between cycles is asked of Codex's app server (`thread/compact/start`), because `/compact` sent as a turn is only text. A failed turn, a stream that ends with no result, a cancelled turn and a mismatched thread each end as a result the loop can read.

Models are resolved once: a brief keeps its model's name, and the operator's equivalences give Astra 6.2 for Fable 5.2 and Sol 6.2 for Opus 5.5; a model with no equivalent is refused before a turn is spent, and the effort is always passed on (the machine's own Codex default is another). The client is chosen at the start and kept: `single_run.py start --client codex`, `brief_run.py start --agent codex` or `--stream-agent b=codex` for a mixed run, `brief_run.py foundation --agent codex`, a brief's `- client:` setting, FEATURE_LOOP_CLIENT. The preflight shows each stream's client, model and effort, and blocks an unmapped model, a Codex stream that would fork a Claude Code conversation, and a Codex that is not given this checkout's CLAUDE.md.

What was tried live on Codex CLI 0.169 before building, on scratch threads: the event format; resume by thread id; compaction through the app server, after which the thread still knew what it had read; and approvals. A headless turn with approval_policy on-request alone cannot ask to leave the sandbox, and added writable folders do not open the repository's store, so a worker in a sibling jj workspace could not commit; `--approve-for-me` (the workspace-write sandbox, requests reviewed automatically) let it, and is what a turn is started with, as the counterpart of the `--permission-mode auto` the loops give Claude Code.

One source for each instruction. Codex reads this repository's CLAUDE.md in place (project_doc_fallback_filenames, on the command line because a fresh sibling workspace is not a trusted project, and in .codex/config.toml). The skills are the files under .claude/skills, reached through relative links in .agents/skills; publish and review-findings, which only the user may start, say so for Codex too (agents/openai.yaml). `agent_client.py instructions --client codex` renders what the model would be given without calling one and checks it (CLAUDE.md's first and last lines present, nothing shadowing it, within the byte budget, each skill linked, no user-only skill offered to a work turn), printing paths, digests and pass or fail; run against the real client here it passes, and the two user-only skills are absent from the list Codex is offered. The three watcher skills now name both models approved for the watcher's role, Opus 5.5 and Sol 6.2, where they told any other model to stop.

Identity, authority and cost. A Codex started from a Claude Code session would inherit that session's identity: the boundary removes it and keeps who started the loop in the binding, and a job is submitted under Codex's own thread. The person-only guards (sync.py allow approve, review accept, the single-agent run's continue message, prune_workspaces) now recognize Codex's mark on the commands it runs as they did Claude Code's, since Codex may give a command a terminal. Codex reports tokens and no dollars, so a Codex turn's cost is unknown and is shown so ($? or $1.50+?, with its tokens) in the progress line, the status bar and the summaries, never as nought.

Not in this commit: Codex sessions in the published traces (sync.py does not read Codex's logs, and must not before the redaction rules cover Codex's account identifiers; the proof of concept's reader and policy 5 are to be ported and the rules stamped), Codex hooks, the proof stages of /prove-java-change, and runtime checkouts. llm-dlc/loops/codex-pilot.md is the small two-stream brief the live rehearsals use.

Verified by 29 new tests over a stand-in for the client (llm-dlc/tools/codex_standin.py): the adapter's 19, a two-cycle single-agent run carried by the stand-in through the real feature-loop.sh (the user's prompt and continue message reach it word for word, the thread is compacted by the client between the cycles and resumed, nothing of the run or of the watcher's identity reaches the worker, and Claude Code runs no turn), a run's choice of client per stream, and unknown costs. The tests of what changed passed, 31 of 31 Python test files (python3 lib/tools/test_costs.py run --changed --rust-jobs 1 under an 8G cap; no Rust input changed), and the files edited after that run started were run again (test_single_run, test_prove_loop, test_agent_client, test_runs, test_loop_stats, test_inbox: all pass). The live two-cycle rehearsals with real Codex workers follow this commit, from workspaces made from it.

commits.summary: Every Codex turn is given its sandbox and approvals, a resumed one too; and a session asks a Codex thread by a tool, not by typing into its terminal
commits.body:
The first live rehearsal of a Codex worker (a Sol 6.2 session on llm-dlc/loops/codex-pilot-a.md through feature-loop.sh, in the disposable workspace codex-pilot-a) found what the stand-in could not: its first cycle wrote its note, committed it with sync.py commit and was compacted through the app server, and its second cycle, a resumed turn, found the workspace read-only with approvals off, changed nothing and said so, so the loop stopped with 'no commit, session needs attention'. Codex's own log shows why: 'codex exec resume' takes no sandbox flag and does not keep the thread's, so a resumed turn falls back to exec's read-only default. agent_client.py now gives every turn, new or resumed, the three settings that --approve-for-me stands for (sandbox_mode workspace-write, approval_policy on-request, approvals_reviewer auto_review); a probe on a scratch repository confirmed that a resumed turn given them writes a file and commits with jj from a sibling workspace.

llm-dlc/tools/ask_codex.py is how a Claude Code session asks a Codex thread a question, after this session's attempt to type one into the expert's tmux window was refused by the permission check, and rightly: a pasted text races the person at that terminal and the answer has to be read off a screen. 'ask --thread NAME --prompt-file FILE' runs one read-only turn of a thread of its own (the first question to a name forks an existing session, which is left as it was, or starts an empty one; later questions resume it) and returns the answer as data with a timeout; the outgoing text goes through the project's redaction rules first and a finding refuses it, since a question leaves the machine; every exchange is kept as a file under llm-dlc/loop-summaries/exchanges. 'mail send|list|read' is a file mailbox for the way back, which a Codex session can write with a shell command, and 'note' leaves a line in a session a person has open (codex queue). An answer or a message is advice for the receiving session to judge, never an instruction or a person's approval, and each says so. The design is the one recommended to this session by the user's session in tmux 4; the permission rule it suggests for the tool is the user's to add, and this commit adds none.

Verified by 7 new tests over the stand-in client (a first question, a fork and a resumed question, a timeout that stops the client, a failed turn, a refused text of which nothing is sent or kept, a queued note, a message's life in a mailbox) and the changed adapter tests, which now require the same three settings on a resumed turn as on the first; the tests of what changed pass, 4 of 4 Python test files (python3 lib/tools/test_costs.py run --changed --rust-jobs 1 under an 8G cap). The live rehearsal is run again from this commit.

commits.summary: A Codex session is traced as a Claude Code session is: its log read as a transcript, its account identifiers and usage redacted (policy 5)
commits.body:
Brief 00, the trace side. Ported from the 2026-11-16 proof of concept onto the current sources: llm-dlc/tools/codex_rollout.py finds the rollouts of the Codex sessions that started in a checkout and gives a rollout's lines as entries shaped like a Claude Code transcript's, one for one and in memory, so sync.py's summary, manifest, metrics and check read both clients with one code path; sync.py takes a session's id from the rollout, names the running session by CODEX_THREAD_ID before Claude Code's variable (a Codex started from a Claude Code session passes that session's variables on), counts apply_patch as an edit, and records manifest.client.tool as codex; metrics.py reads a command's or a patch's result from the same line. The three-way merge of sync.py had one conflict, an import line.

Redaction policy 5 removes what Codex records about the account: the identifiers under creator_user_id, creator_account_id, chatgpt_user_id and chatgpt_account_id, under those keys and inside strings, and the account usage object rate_limits (plan, credit balance, limits), which is replaced whole. It comes before any Codex log is stored. The rules changed, so they were stamped as CLAUDE.md prescribes, with 'sync.py stamp --equivalent': 303,536 distinct lines give the same results under the rules at the parent commit, so the stamp keeps its date and no published log changes. The test's account value is made up (the proof of concept's looked real and was not copied).

commits.summary: The time and loop statistics read a session Codex carried: its record names the thread, a model call has its real start, and an unknown cost is not nought
commits.body:
Brief 00, asked for by the user before any real run: until now a loop that Codex carried was traced, but the statistics could not find it. Codex traces a session under its own thread id, not the id the loop gave it, so feature-loop.sh now writes 'Codex thread THREAD carries session SESSION.' into its record once the thread exists (in the header for a session that is continued, after the first turn for a new one; 'agent_client.py thread' prints it), and loop_stats.py, sync.py's publishing of run records and tool_time.py's discovery take the thread for the session where the record has that line.

Three things would have made the numbers wrong. A Codex response's items are written to the log together when it ends, so a model call looked a few milliseconds long: codex_rollout.claude_view gives each call the time the model was handed the turn (a prompt, a tool call's output, a compaction) and metrics.py starts the call there. Codex's model calls a tool that runs commands, and the log has the call and each command: tool_time.py takes the commands for the calls where a batch has them, so a wait is counted once and filed by what ran. And a model with no row in pricing.json summed to $0.00: the statistics page prints such a cost as '?' or '$1.50+?' and names the runs in a note.

Checked on the real log and records of the Astra rehearsal before its workspace was removed: two runs found by their records (2 cycles with 2 commits, then 1 cycle with none), 418 s of the first prompt's 418 s accounted for (404 s the model, 20 s tools; it was 4 s of model time before), the commit's 19 s filed under sync.py, every cost shown as '?'. The three rehearsal workspaces (codex-pilot-a, codex-pilot-a-claude, codex-single) are forgotten, their commits abandoned and their folders removed, at the user's word.

Verified by five new tests and two extended ones (a Codex-carried run in loop_stats with its record line and without, the cost cells, a rollout read by tool_time with wrapper and commands, the call's start in test_codex, the record line through the real feature-loop.sh in test_single_run, 'thread' in test_agent_client); the tests of what changed pass, 23 of 23 Python test files (python3 lib/tools/test_costs.py run --changed --rust-jobs 1 under an 8G cap).

commits.summary: Codex sessions get the checkout's two hooks: the adapter runs them after each turn it carried, and .codex/hooks.json names them for a trusted checkout
commits.body:
Brief 00. Claude Code runs two hook commands from .claude/settings.json: 'sync.py hook' at a turn's end (finished turns to Langfuse, where that is set up) and 'sync.py hook-commit' after a shell command (a commit made without sync.py gets its session's trace). A Codex session had neither. Both commands now take Codex's payload, whose transcript_path is the session's rollout: the session id is read from the rollout's name, and a Codex log is sent to Langfuse read whole, each prompt remembered by an id made of its turn and line (codex_rollout.claude_view gives prompts that id), so no turn is sent twice.

Where they run from was the question. Codex loads a project's hooks only from a project a person trusted, and runs only hooks a person reviewed; a loop's worker runs in a fresh sibling workspace, which is neither. Probes from a scratch folder (Codex CLI 0.169) showed: hooks given with -c run only with --dangerously-bypass-hook-trust; a project's .codex/hooks.json did not run even with that flag and a trust_level given with -c ('Untrusted project-local configuration is disabled'); a hook's command goes through a shell. The bypass flag would also run every other unreviewed hook, so agent_client.py runs the two commands itself after each Codex turn, with the payload Codex's hooks get: hook-commit when a command of the turn made a plain commit, then hook. A failure is written beside the attempt (*.hooks.log) and stops nothing; AGENT_CLIENT_HOOKS=off turns it off. .codex/hooks.json names the same two commands for a session a person runs in a trusted checkout; that Codex loads that file was not verified, since it needs a person's review in /hooks (the same definitions ran when given inline, and both commands pass a pipe-test with status 0 and no output).

Verified by a real Codex turn through agent_client.py in a scratch jj repository with a recording stand-in for sync.py: both commands ran, given the real rollout named by the thread; by four new tests (the Stop payload and the commit hook through the stand-in, a hook that fails, the two hook files naming the same commands, a Codex log sent turn by turn by hook_export); and by the tests of what changed, 21 of 21 Python test files (python3 lib/tools/test_costs.py run --changed --rust-jobs 1 under an 8G cap).

commits.summary: A Codex turn's own compactions reach the loop, and a decision in the allow list that no person took is an error of check
commits.body:
Two things brief 00 had left open, taken up at the user's word and settled by probes of Codex CLI 0.169 from scratch folders (2026-11-19).

Automatic compaction in the middle of a turn: 'codex exec --json' prints nothing for one (a turn made to compact five times showed only its items), but the thread's log gets a 'compacted' line each time, with the size of the context it replaced. agent_client.py now reads the log as the turn goes (what was appended since the turn began, at each event and at the end) and prints Claude Code's compact_boundary for each, so a moonshot's compaction with no commit is put to its watcher under either client. The translation of a guessed stream event is gone, the stand-in compacts as Codex does, and the trace's boundary carries the size too. The loop's FEATURE_LOOP_AUTOCOMPACT is not passed to Codex: it is a size for Claude Code's window, and Codex keeps the model's own threshold.

The allow list and the reviewed findings: Codex's sandbox cannot keep them from a patch in a way the tools survive. A file marked 'read' in a permission profile was patched all the same (the automatic reviewer let the request through, as it did for the built-in read-only profile), and one marked 'deny' could not be read by any command, the repository's own tool included, with no way to ask. So the bar is in the tool, for every client: the three commands a person runs (approve and add of the allow list, accept of a review) record each decision they wrote on the machine (person-decisions.json in the state folder, a digest and never the value), and check reports as an error a decision in either file that is neither in the file as published (the newest immutable ancestors of @, asked only when the files change) nor in that record. A person who did take one says so with a new command, vouch, of the allow list, which agents are refused (the tool's own check, a deny rule in .claude/settings.json, a forbidden rule for Codex). The record is a file an agent could write: it catches a mistake or a habit, not a forgery. On this checkout every approved entry is published, so the check finds nothing.

Verified by five new tests (a compaction read from a log once and only if it is the turn's; an approval a person made against one written by hand; a published decision and the cached answer; vouching; an accepted finding) and the changed ones (the adapter through the stand-in over three turns); test_review.py now keeps its state in a folder of its own, since a person's command writes the record. The tests of what changed pass, 23 of 23 Python test files (python3 lib/tools/test_costs.py run --changed --rust-jobs 1 under an 8G cap). The default test run on the merge before this commit passed, 58 of 58 (recorded for tree 93f833f7a9f1).

commits.summary: A failed turn or compaction ends a loop needing attention, and a single agent's run is checked at its start, its restart and its landing
commits.body:
An outside review of the Codex work found four things; this takes up what bears on a single agent's run, with the user's decisions of 2026-11-19 (the rule for failed turns holds for every loop; the network is open to Codex workers; list prices for the two Codex models).

A turn that did not end well is not a cycle. feature-loop.sh only logged a worker turn the client had ended with an error (a quota, an interruption) or cut off, and on the last cycle of a count it then skipped the watcher's verdict, compacted, summarized and exited 0; a failed compaction was logged and ignored. It now reads the turn's own event stream: no result, or a result that is not a success, stops the loop with status 1 and a record line that says the session needs attention, before any compaction or summary; a compaction that fails stops it too, after the summary when the run was ending anyway. A turn that ends well with no commit is judged as before. Claude Code's own compaction shows as a boundary in its stream (seen in the logs of earlier runs), which the rule takes for success.

A single run's start and restart. A Codex run now gets the check a brief's Codex streams get, in the agent's folder: the client is there and is given the checkout's CLAUDE.md whole. A restart keeps the count of cycles and the queue's setting of the leg before unless given its own (--cycles N, 0 for none; --verification) and prints what it kept; before, a bare restart dropped the count and turned the queue back on. A restart of a Codex run whose record names a thread, and whose binding is gone, is refused: a new thread would be told to go on with work it never saw.

Decisions only a person takes. One that no person is recorded as having taken now waives nothing (the redactor is given only published or recorded decisions, so the finding stays raised), a new question of sync.py (decisions, with --at REV for a commit) says which there are, and landing a workspace's line asks it first and leaves the line where it is. A push already refuses while check has the error. The user's own approval of b24f7c44, made in their terminal while this was written, left its record and the check finds nothing: the legitimate path works.

Also: the network is open inside a Codex worker's sandbox (probed: a host is not resolved without the setting, reached with it); AGENT_CLIENT_CODEX_SETTINGS gives a rehearsal extra client settings; OpenAI's list prices for gpt-6.2-astra and gpt-6.2-sol are in pricing.json (from developers.openai.com/api/docs/pricing, 2026-11-19), with the rates of a prompt over 272K tokens, which metrics.py applies per call; the Stop hook of .codex/hooks.json shows a message while it runs.

Verified by eight new tests and the changed ones: through single_run.py with a one-cycle cap and the Codex stand-in, a turn that fails, one that is cut off, a compaction that fails and a quiet turn that ends well; a restart's kept limits; the instruction check and the lost thread; an unrecorded decision that waives nothing and a line that is asked; landing refused and then allowed; the long-context price. The tests of what changed pass, 26 of 26 Python test files (python3 lib/tools/test_costs.py run --changed --rust-jobs 1 under an 8G cap).
