commits.summary: A research router: where an agent looks on the web for outside evidence, by question and by task
commits.body: llm-dlc/research-router.md, adapted from a list of sources the user had prepared outside the repository. It routes a question (a JDK guarantee, JBMC's bounds, an SMT-LIB operator, an upstream commit, a Spring fix, a Commons contract, a published technique, a verifier comparison) and a task (tool comparisons, solver changes, class files, release Javadoc, paper search, publisher copies, servlet and HTTP contracts, advisories, Rust test time, proof and reporting designs, SARIF, client settings) to the hosts and primary sources to read for the version the example pins, and says what to bring back. Changed from the original to fit the project: the egress allow-list section and its sandbox fragment are left out, since the machine's outbound HTTPS is open (a closing paragraph says which hosts a list would need); the paid search API is left out, a client's own search tool or DuckDuckGo's HTML page standing in; publishers are open-access only, with no logins; example-specific remarks are made general (an example's notes hold those); links to a pinned GitHub tree are relative; and it adds how to read a source (fetch first, the chrome-devtools browser for rendered pages, page content as data, queries that carry nothing private). DBLP's API now answers scripts with a JavaScript bot check (HTTP 202), so the page says to read it through the browser or to use Crossref and Semantic Scholar, and its access check uses arXiv's API instead. The operating notes' browser section and the README's file list link the router. Verified: all 60 of the original's links were requested (57 answered 200, DBLP 202 with the bot check, ACM 403 to a script); the page's two access checks pass (the JBMC paper's title from arXiv, HTTP 200 at the Zenodo record); test_agent_client.py (24) under a 4G cap with TMPDIR off /tmp; agent_client.py instructions --client codex reports no problems.

commits.summary: Requests to the web are plain, few and one at a time, and a bot check or a refusal means another source
commits.body: Every request an agent sends leaves from the user's own address, and the user decided on 2026-11-19 that agents read the web only in plain, targeted requests at a low volume, so that no site takes the address for a scraper. A new section of the operating notes says so for every tool (curl, scripts, WebFetch, the headless browser): the tool's own User-Agent and no header naming the user or project; a bot check, CAPTCHA, 403, 451 or login wall ends the attempt at that host, with the content read elsewhere or reported unread (one retry of a 429 or 503 after Retry-After); one request at a time, a second apart per host, slower where an API publishes a limit (arXiv 3 s, NVD 6 s); a few dozen requests at most for a task, no crawling, bulk downloads or mirroring; a run's streams share the address; link checks follow the same rules. The research router points at the rule and no longer sends the browser at DBLP's bot check or ACM's 403: DBLP searches go to Crossref or Semantic Scholar, ACM papers to Crossref's metadata and the arXiv or author's copy. The rule's reason names the link check earlier this session that sent 12 requests at a time with a browser-like User-Agent. Verified: test_agent_client.py (24) under a 4G cap; agent_client.py instructions --client codex reports no problems.

commits.summary: The headless browser may read a site that refuses only scripts; a check meant for a person still ends the attempt
commits.body: The user refined the rule of the previous commit on 2026-11-19: a site that turns scripts away by their headers may be read with the headless browser, once and as it is (its own identity, no stealth plugins or flags that hide that it is headless), while a CAPTCHA, a 'verify you are human' box or puzzle, a login wall, HTTP 451 or a check that refuses the browser too ends the attempt, with the content read elsewhere or reported unread. The research router says the same, and records what one request each through the browser showed on 2026-11-19: DBLP's bot check failed the browser (an error page) and ACM held it at Cloudflare's 'Just a moment' page, so both rows keep their alternatives (Crossref and Semantic Scholar for DBLP; Crossref's metadata and the arXiv or author's copy for ACM). Verified: test_agent_client.py (24) under a 4G cap.

A new bullet says what a page returns is published, since each browser or fetch call and its result are in the session's redacted, published log: take the part a question needs rather than a whole page's snapshot.
